title: A Survey on the Memory Mechanism of Large Language Model-based Agents
authors_or_org: Zeyu Zhang, Xiaohe Bo, Chen Ma, Rui Li, Xu Chen, Quanyu Dai, Jieming Zhu, Zhenhua Dong, Ji-Rong Wen
summary: The most-cited systematic survey of memory in LLM-based agents. Defines what agent memory is and why it is needed, then reviews memory sources, forms, and operations, plus evaluation methods (direct and indirect) and downstream applications. Maintains a living repository of memory papers.
key_claims: Organises memory design along sources (inside-trial, cross-trial, external knowledge), forms (textual vs parametric) and operations (writing, management, reading)
Distinguishes direct memory evaluation (subjective/objective metrics on memory content) from indirect evaluation via downstream task performance
759 citations as indexed by Consensus, making it the anchor reference for agent-memory taxonomy
relevance: The canonical taxonomy (source x form x operation) that most later coding-agent memory papers cite; supplies the write/manage/read vocabulary used throughout the memory track.

title: Rethinking Memory in LLM based Agents: Representations, Operations, and Emerging Topics
authors_or_org: Yiming Du, Wenyu Huang, Danna Zheng, Zhaowei Wang, Sebastien Montella, Mirella Lapata, Kam-Fai Wong, Jeff Z. Pan
summary: Proposes the operations-first taxonomy of agent memory: memory is either parametric (in weights) or contextual (external, structured or unstructured), and is acted on by six atomic operations. Maps these onto four research topics: long-term memory, long-context, parametric modification, multi-source memory.
key_claims: Six atomic memory operations: Consolidation, Updating, Indexing, Forgetting, Retrieval, Condensation
Parametric vs contextual (structured/unstructured) is the primary representation split
Existing surveys over-emphasise applications and under-specify the operations governing memory dynamics
relevance: Supplies the write/consolidate/retrieve/forget operation axis that the memory track uses to code who writes memory and when.

title: Memory in the Age of AI Agents
summary: Argues the long/short-term dichotomy is insufficient and re-frames agent memory through forms, functions and dynamics. Explicitly separates agent memory from LLM memory, RAG and context engineering, and compiles benchmarks and open-source frameworks.
key_claims: Three forms of agent memory: token-level, parametric, and latent
Three functions: factual, experiential, and working memory
Dynamics axis covers how memory is formed, evolved and retrieved over time
Names memory automation, RL integration, multi-agent memory and trustworthiness as frontiers
relevance: The cleanest recent taxonomy separating experiential memory (what coding agents need) from factual/personalisation memory (what most benchmarks measure).

title: Memory for Autonomous LLM Agents: Mechanisms, Evaluation, and Emerging Frontiers
summary: Formalises agent memory as a write-manage-read loop coupled to perception and action, with a three-dimensional taxonomy over temporal scope, representational substrate and control policy. Covers 2022 to early 2026 and explicitly includes coding agents as an application area.
key_claims: Five mechanism families: context-resident compression, retrieval-augmented stores, reflective self-improvement, hierarchical virtual context, policy-learned management
Traces evaluation shift from static recall benchmarks to multi-session agentic tests
Engineering realities named: write-path filtering, contradiction handling, latency budgets, privacy governance
Open challenges: continual consolidation, causally grounded retrieval, trustworthy reflection, learned forgetting
relevance: Closest survey to this track's framing: write-manage-read loop plus an explicit coding-agent application section.

title: A Survey of Agent Memory in the Second Half: Towards Self-Evolving and Long-Horizon Agents
summary: Unifies agent memory along three dimensions (substrate, cognitive mechanism, subject) and argues memory is the substrate through which agents self-evolve. Explicitly names agentic coding as a driving long-horizon setting.
key_claims: Three dimensions: memory substrate (internal parametric vs external retrieval-augmented), cognitive mechanism (sensory, working, episodic, semantic, procedural), memory subject (user-centric vs agent-centric)
Hundreds of agent-memory papers released in 2025 alone
Memory management is itself becoming a trainable capability (RL-learned context curation, decision-time consolidation)
Identifies portable, shareable agent skills as an emerging ecosystem
relevance: Directly links persistent memory to the agent-skills ecosystem that coding harnesses now ship, and to RL-trained memory management.

title: Anatomy of Agentic Memory: Taxonomy and Empirical Analysis of Evaluation and System Limitations
summary: Critical survey arguing the empirical foundations of agentic memory are fragile: benchmarks are undersized and saturating, metrics misalign with semantic utility, results are backbone-dependent, and system-level costs are ignored.
key_claims: Taxonomy of memory-augmented generation systems by four memory structures
Names benchmark saturation, judge sensitivity, backbone-dependent accuracy, and maintenance latency/throughput overhead as the four pain points
Argues current agentic memory systems underperform their theoretical promise
relevance: The strongest sceptical counterweight: evidence that headline memory-system gains are fragile and cost-blind.

title: Cognitive Architectures for Language Agents
authors_or_org: Theodore R. Sumers, Shunyu Yao, Karthik Narasimhan, Thomas L. Griffiths
summary: CoALA proposes a cognitive-architecture framework for language agents with modular memory (working, episodic, semantic, procedural), a structured action space split into internal (memory) and external (environment) actions, and a generalised decision procedure.
key_claims: Memory modules: working, episodic, semantic, procedural
Internal actions are reasoning, retrieval and learning (writing to long-term memory); external actions are grounding
Retrospectively organises prior language-agent work and prospectively identifies gaps
relevance: The foundational framing most coding-agent memory papers inherit: memory writes are first-class internal actions, not side effects.

title: Externalization in LLM Agents: A Unified Review of Memory, Skills, Protocols and Harness Engineering
summary: Reviews the shift from weights to context to harness through the lens of externalization: memory externalizes state across time, skills externalize procedural expertise, protocols externalize interaction structure, and the harness coordinates them.
key_claims: Memory, skills and protocols are three distinct but coupled forms of externalization
Harness engineering is the unification layer that turns externalized modules into governed execution
Identifies self-evolving harnesses and shared agent infrastructure as emerging directions
relevance: Explicitly joins the memory track to the harness track: memory as one of several externalized cognitive artifacts the harness governs.

title: Experience Compression Spectrum: Unifying Memory, Skills, and Rules in LLM Agents
authors_or_org: Xing Zhang, Guanghui Wang, Yanwei Cui, Wei Qiu, Ziyuan Li, Bing Zhu, Peiyang He
summary: Unifies memory, skills and rules on a single axis of increasing compression, and documents that the agent-memory and skill-discovery communities barely cite each other.
key_claims: Citation overlap between the memory and skill literatures is below 1% across 1,136 references
Compression ratios: episodic memory 5-20x, procedural skills 50-500x, declarative rules 1000x+
Existing systems operate at a fixed compression level with no adaptive capability - the 'missing diagonal'
Knowledge lifecycle management remains largely neglected; evaluation couples tightly to compression level
relevance: Provides the single best organising axis for this track: memory vs skills vs rules are the same artifact at different compression, and nobody manages the lifecycle.

title: MemGPT: Towards LLMs as Operating Systems
authors_or_org: Charles Packer, Sarah Wooders, Kevin Lin, Vivian Fang, Shishir G. Patil, Ion Stoica, Joseph E. Gonzalez
summary: MemGPT introduces virtual context management: an OS-style hierarchy of main context (in-window) and external context, with the LLM itself issuing function calls to page data in and out and to edit its own core memory. Evaluated on document analysis and multi-session chat.
key_claims: Virtual context management lets an agent analyse documents far exceeding its context window
The agent self-edits persistent core memory via tool calls, making memory writes agent-initiated actions
Became the reference architecture for tiered agent memory and the basis of the Letta platform
relevance: Foundational: establishes agent-initiated self-editing memory and the OS metaphor that coding harnesses reuse for CLAUDE.md-style stores.

title: Mem0: Building Production-Ready AI Agents with Scalable Long-Term Memory
authors_or_org: Prateek Chhikara, Dev Khant, Saket Aryan, Taranjeet Singh, Deshraj Yadav
summary: The Mem0 paper introduces a memory-centric architecture that dynamically extracts, consolidates and retrieves salient information from ongoing conversations, plus a graph-based variant, evaluated on LoCoMo against full-context and other memory systems.
key_claims: 26% relative improvement in the LLM-as-a-Judge metric over OpenAI's memory on LoCoMo
Graph memory variant adds approximately 2% overall performance
91% lower p95 latency versus full-context approaches
Saves more than 90% token cost relative to processing entire conversation histories
Evaluated across single-hop, temporal, multi-hop and open-domain question categories
26% relative improvement on LLM-as-a-Judge over OpenAI memory baseline
Graph variant adds roughly 2% over the base configuration
91% lower p95 latency and over 90% token-cost saving versus the full-context method
relevance: The most-cited memory-platform benchmark claim, and the one whose contested status makes it the anchor for the memory-evaluation-credibility section.

verification.notes: Chhikara et al., 28 Apr 2025. Abstract confirms 26% relative improvement over OpenAI on LoCoMo, 91% lower p95 latency, >90% token savings.

title: Zep: A Temporal Knowledge Graph Architecture for Agent Memory
authors_or_org: Preston Rasmussen, Pavlo Paliychuk, Travis Beauvais, Jack Ryan, Daniel Chalef
summary: Zep is a memory service built on Graphiti, a time-aware knowledge graph engine that integrates conversational and business data while preserving temporal relationships, evaluated on DMR and LongMemEval.
key_claims: DMR benchmark: 94.8% accuracy versus MemGPT's 93.4%
LongMemEval: up to 18.5% accuracy improvement with 90% latency reduction versus baseline
Emphasis on enterprise tasks such as cross-session synthesis and sustained context maintenance
94.8% vs 93.4% for MemGPT on the Deep Memory Retrieval benchmark
Up to 18.5% accuracy improvement on LongMemEval with 90% lower response latency versus baseline implementations
Gains concentrate on cross-session synthesis and long-term context maintenance
relevance: The knowledge-graph pole of memory architecture, and the source of the 84% family of claims later disputed — useful for the benchmark-credibility discussion.

verification.notes: Rasmussen et al., 20 Jan 2025. Abstract confirms DMR 94.8% vs 93.4% and LongMemEval up to 18.5% accuracy gain / 90% latency reduction.

title: A-MEM: Agentic Memory for LLM Agents
authors_or_org: Wujiang Xu, Zujie Liang, Kai Mei, Hang Gao, Juntao Tan, Yongfeng Zhang
summary: A-MEM applies the Zettelkasten method to agent memory: each new memory becomes a structured note with contextual description, keywords and tags, is linked to related historical notes, and can trigger updates to the attributes of those earlier notes (memory evolution).
key_claims: Dynamic indexing and linking produce an interconnected knowledge network rather than a flat store
Adding a memory can retroactively evolve existing memories' representations
Superior to SOTA baselines across six foundation models
relevance: The reference 'agentic' write policy where the agent, not a fixed pipeline, decides structure and links - directly analogous to an agent maintaining its own repo notes.

verification.notes: Xu et al., v1 17 Feb 2025. Abstract confirms Zettelkasten dynamic indexing/linking, memory evolution, six foundation models.

title: MemoryBank: Enhancing Large Language Models with Long-Term Memory
authors_or_org: Wanjun Zhong, Lianghong Guo, Qiqi Gao, He Ye, Yanlin Wang
summary: MemoryBank stores, summarises and retrieves conversational memories and updates retention using a mechanism modelled on the Ebbinghaus forgetting curve, so memories decay or are reinforced by elapsed time and significance.
key_claims: First widely-cited use of an explicit forgetting curve as the memory-retention policy
Builds a user-personality profile by synthesising past interactions
Demonstrated via the SiliconFriend companion chatbot
relevance: Foundational for the forget/expiry operation - the least-implemented operation in coding-agent memory stores.

title: Generative Agents: Interactive Simulacra of Human Behavior
authors_or_org: Joon Sung Park, Joseph C. O'Brien, Carrie J. Cai, Meredith Ringel Morris, Percy Liang, Michael S. Bernstein
summary: Introduces the memory stream: a complete natural-language record of an agent's experiences, retrieved by a recency/importance/relevance score, and periodically synthesised into higher-level reflections that feed planning.
key_claims: Memory stream + retrieval + reflection + planning architecture
Ablation shows observation, planning and reflection each contribute critically to believability
Reflection is the mechanism that turns raw episodic logs into reusable abstractions
relevance: Origin of the reflection operation (episode-level write timing) that ReasoningBank, SWE-Exp and MemCoder all descend from.

title: MemOS: A Memory OS for AI System
authors_or_org: Zhiyu Li, Feiyu Xiong, Huajun Chen et al. (MemTensor)
summary: MemOS proposes a memory operating system that treats memory as a manageable system resource, unifying plaintext, activation-based and parameter-level memory in MemCubes that encapsulate content plus metadata such as provenance and versioning. Submitted 2025-07-04, last revised 2025-12-03.
key_claims: MemCubes 'encapsulate both memory content and metadata such as provenance and versioning', enabling transitions between memory types
Unifies plaintext, activation-based and parameter-level memory under one scheduling abstraction
Argues LLMs lack 'well-defined memory management systems', hindering long-context reasoning and personalization
Three memory types unified: parametric, activation, plaintext
MemCube is the standardised unit carrying provenance and versioning metadata
Explicit lifecycle control and governance, absent from RAG which it calls a stateless workaround
relevance: The most ambitious taxonomy of memory substrates (context vs activation vs weights), useful as the conceptual frame against which shipping products are only covering the plaintext tier.

verification.notes: Li et al., 4 Jul 2025 (rev 3 Dec 2025). Abstract confirms MemCube, plaintext/activation/parameter memory unification.

title: LightMem: Lightweight and Efficient Memory-Augmented Generation
authors_or_org: Jizhan Fang, Xinle Deng, Haoming Xu, Ziyan Jiang, Yuqi Tang, Ziwen Xu, Shumin Deng, Yunzhi Yao, Mengru Wang, Shuofei Qiao, Huajun Chen, Ningyu Zhang
summary: LightMem organises memory in three Atkinson-Shiffrin-inspired stages: sensory-memory filtering and topic grouping, topic-aware short-term consolidation, and long-term memory with a sleep-time (offline) update that decouples consolidation from online inference.
key_claims: Up to 7.7% / 29.3% QA accuracy improvement on LongMemEval / LoCoMo over strong baselines
Up to 38x / 20.9x total token reduction and 30x / 55.5x fewer API calls
Purely online test-time cost drops up to 106x / 117x in tokens and 159x / 310x in API calls
relevance: The strongest quantitative case that moving consolidation offline (sleep-time) is what makes persistent memory affordable.

title: Memori: A Persistent Memory Layer for Efficient, Context-Aware LLM Agents
authors_or_org: Luiz C. Borro, Luiz A. B. Macarini, Gordon Tindall, Michael Montero, Adam B. Struck
summary: Memori is a system-agnostic persistent memory layer that treats memory as a data-structuring problem, converting dialogue into compact semantic triples plus conversation summaries rather than storing raw transcripts.
key_claims: ~82% accuracy on LoCoMo using only 1,294 tokens per query, about 5% of full-context requirements
67% fewer tokens than competing memory approaches
Over 20x cost saving versus exhaustive-context methods
Structured representation beats simply expanding the context window for practical deployment
relevance: Direct evidence on the representation question: structured triples beat both raw context and less-structured memory on cost per unit of recall.

verification.notes: Borro et al., 20 Mar 2026. Abstract confirms 81.95% LoCoMo accuracy at 1,294 tokens/query (~5% of full context) and 67% fewer tokens than competitors.

title: MemMachine: A Ground-Truth-Preserving Memory System for Personalized AI Agents
summary: MemMachine stores whole conversational episodes to avoid lossy LLM-based extraction, then layers contextualized retrieval that expands nucleus matches with surrounding context. Includes a six-dimension ablation isolating retrieval-stage versus ingestion-stage gains.
key_claims: 0.9169 on LoCoMo with gpt4.1-mini; 93.0% on LongMemEval-S
Retrieval-stage optimisations dominate ingestion-stage ones: retrieval-depth tuning +4.2%, context formatting +2.0%, search-prompt design +1.8%, query-bias correction +1.4% vs sentence chunking +0.8%
Roughly 80% fewer input tokens than Mem0 under matched conditions
relevance: Quantifies that read-path design matters more than write-path extraction - a direct finding on where memory engineering effort pays off.

verification.notes: Wang et al., 6 Apr 2026. Abstract confirms LoCoMo 0.9169, LongMemEvalS 93.0%, ~80% fewer input tokens vs Mem0.

title: Agent Memory: Characterization and System Implications of Stateful Long-Horizon Workloads
summary: First systems-level characterization of agent memory: a four-axis system-oriented taxonomy, a phase-aware profiling harness attributing cost to construction, retrieval and generation, and measurement of ten representative systems across two benchmark suites.
key_claims: Ten representative memory systems profiled across construction, retrieval and generation phases
Derives 10 system recommendations covering construction scheduling, capability floors, amortization via query volume, freshness-latency tradeoffs and fleet-scale management
Design choices shift cost between the write path and the read path rather than eliminating it
relevance: Supplies the cost model for memory as infrastructure - essential for arguing about whether repo memory pays for itself.

title: Is Agent Memory a Database? Rethinking Data Foundations for Long-Term AI Agent Memory
summary: Vision paper arguing long-term agent memory is a new data-management workload whose correctness is a property of the state trajectory, not of individual records. Formalises Governed Evolving Memory (GEM) with four state-level operators and six correctness conditions.
key_claims: Four recurring failure modes: unregulated growth, missing semantic revision, capacity-driven forgetting, read-only retrieval
Four state-level operators: ingestion, revision, forgetting, retrieval
Proves no record-level system can satisfy the six correctness conditions regardless of storage model
Prototype MemState on a property-graph backend
relevance: Best articulation of why append-only markdown memory files degrade: correctness lives in the trajectory, not the record.

verification.notes: Orogat & Mansour, 25 May 2026. Abstract confirms four failure modes, the GEM formalisation with four state-level operators and six correctness conditions, and the MemState prototype.

title: Beyond the Context Window: A Cost-Performance Analysis of Fact-Based Memory vs. Long-Context LLMs for Persistent Agents
summary: Compares a Mem0-based fact memory against long-context inference on LongMemEval, LoCoMo and PersonaMemv2 on both accuracy and cumulative API cost, with a cost model incorporating prompt caching.
key_claims: Long-context GPT-5-mini achieves higher factual recall on LongMemEval and LoCoMo; the memory system is competitive on PersonaMemv2

The two architectures have structurally different cost profiles: long-context per-turn charge grows with context length even under caching, while memory read cost stays roughly fixed after a one-time write phase
At 100k-token context the memory system becomes cheaper after approximately ten interaction turns, with break-even falling as context grows
Long-context GPT-5-mini achieves higher factual recall than the memory system on LongMemEval and LoCoMo
Memory wins on PersonaMemv2 where stable factual attributes suit flat extraction
At 100k-token context the memory system becomes cheaper after roughly ten interaction turns; break-even shrinks as context grows
relevance: Gives the explicit break-even criterion (≈10 turns at 100k context) for when memory is worth its write cost — directly transferable to a multi-session repo agent.

verification.notes: Pollertlam & Kornsuwannawit, 5 Mar 2026. Abstract confirms ~10-turn break-even at 100k context.

title: Sleep-time Compute: Beyond Inference Scaling at Test-time
authors_or_org: Kevin Lin, Charlie Snell, Yu Wang, Charles Packer, Sarah Wooders, Ion Stoica, Joseph E. Gonzalez
summary: Introduces sleep-time compute: letting a model think offline about a context before queries arrive, pre-computing useful quantities so test-time compute drops. Includes a case study applying it to a realistic agentic SWE task.
key_claims: ~5x reduction in test-time compute for equal accuracy on Stateful GSM-Symbolic and Stateful AIME
Scaling sleep-time compute further raises accuracy by up to 13% and 18% respectively
Amortizing across related queries cuts average cost per query 2.5x
Efficacy correlates with predictability of the user query
relevance: The mechanism behind offline consolidation for coding agents: pre-digest the repo when idle so the next session starts warm.

title: Auto-Dreamer: Learning Offline Memory Consolidation for Language Agents
summary: Auto-Dreamer decouples fast per-session memory acquisition from slow cross-session consolidation, training a consolidator with GRPO using end-to-end agent performance as reward. The consolidator inspects a working region plus provenance-linked source trajectories and synthesizes a compact replacement set.
key_claims: Outperforms fixed, RL-trained and prompted memory baselines on ScienceWorld by 7 points
Uses an active memory bank 12x smaller than the strongest baseline
Transfers to held-out ALFWorld and WebArena without retraining, using 6x less memory on ALFWorld
Consolidation is learned, not heuristic, and is rewarded by downstream task success
relevance: Strongest evidence that consolidation should be a learned, downstream-rewarded offline process rather than a summarisation heuristic.

verification.notes: Ye et al., 20 May 2026. Abstract confirms +7 points on ScienceWorld with a 12x smaller active bank and held-out transfer.

title: Agentic Context Engineering: Evolving Contexts for Self-Improving Language Models
summary: ACE treats contexts as evolving playbooks that accumulate, refine and organize strategies through generation, reflection and curation, using structured incremental updates ('delta' edits) rather than wholesale rewriting.
key_claims: Names two failure modes of naive context evolution: brevity bias (dropping domain insight for concise summaries) and context collapse (iterative rewriting erodes detail)
+10.6% on agent benchmarks and +8.6% on finance over strong baselines
Adapts without labelled supervision, using natural execution feedback
Matches the top-ranked production agent on the AppWorld leaderboard with a smaller open-source model
relevance: Defines context collapse - the central risk when an agent keeps rewriting its own CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md - and the incremental-delta fix.

title: MemReader: From Passive to Active Extraction for Long-Term Agent Memory
summary: MemReader reframes memory extraction as an active decision: a 4B model trained with GRPO evaluates information value, reference ambiguity and completeness before deciding to write, defer, retrieve more context, or discard.
key_claims: One-shot passive extraction causes memory pollution, low-value writes and inconsistency
MemReader-4B is SOTA on knowledge updating, temporal reasoning and hallucination reduction across LOCOMO, LongMemEval and HaluMem
Effective memory requires reasoning-driven selective extraction, not extracting more
Integrated into MemOS and deployed in production
relevance: Directly on write-timing: a learned gate on whether to write at all, which coding agents currently lack.

title: Enhancing Software Engineering Through Closed-Loop Memory Optimization (MemOp)
summary: MemOp is a closed-loop framework for memory augmentation in SE agents that grounds memory utility in validated downstream impact, making utility serve simultaneously as a task-agnostic evaluation benchmark and an annotation-free optimization signal. Evaluated on single-episode and cross-episode memory augmentation.
key_claims: SE agents remain fundamentally episodic: they reconstruct context from scratch and reproduce similar mistakes
Absolute gains of up to +5.25% in success rate and +4.63% in resolve efficiency
Reduces computational cost by at least 9.79%
Defines a principled task-agnostic memory utility that lets memory be evaluated rigorously across agents and settings
Absolute gains up to +5.25% in success rate and +4.63% in resolve efficiency
Computational cost reduced by at least 9.79%
Complementary evaluation on single-episode and cross-episode memory augmentation
relevance: The most direct answer to 'how do we know repo memory is worth writing': validated downstream impact as both metric and training signal.

verification.notes: arXiv:2606.05646 exists (Guo, Wang, Wang, Neubig, Wang). Abstract verbatim contains +5.25% success, +4.63% resolve efficiency, >=9.79% cost reduction. Note: no '-12.5pp action-level' figure exists in the paper or in this record.

title: Your Code Agent Can Grow Alongside You with Structured Memory
authors_or_org: Yi-Xuan Deng, Xiaoqin Liu, Yi Zhang, Guo-Wei Yang, Shuojin Yang
summary: MemCoder structures historical human experience to distil latent intent-to-code mappings from past commits, uses a verification-feedback-driven self-refinement mechanism to correct agent behaviour in real time, and crystallizes human-validated solutions into long-term knowledge through an experience self-internalization mechanism. On SWE-bench Verified it reports state-of-the-art performance and a 9.4% improvement in resolved rate over the general foundation model DeepSeek-V3.2.
key_claims: Distils intent-to-code mappings from past human commits rather than from agent traces alone
Crystallizes human-validated solutions into long-term knowledge via experience self-internalization
9.4% improvement in resolved rate over DeepSeek-V3.2 on SWE-bench Verified
Frames the contribution as continual human-AI co-evolution
Existing code agents are tethered to static code snapshots and ignore the temporal evolution of projects
9.4% improvement in resolved rate over the DeepSeek-V3.2 foundation model on SWE-bench Verified, reported as SOTA
Human-validated solutions, not agent-only outputs, are what get internalized into long-term memory
relevance: The clearest instance of human work products (commits) being mined as the seed of agent memory, with human validation as the promotion criterion.

verification.notes: Paper, title, SWE-bench Verified +9.4% resolved-rate gain over DeepSeek-V3.2 all confirmed on arXiv:2603.13258. Author name is wrong: first author is Yi-Xuan Deng (full list: Yi-Xuan Deng, Xiaoqin Liu, Yi Zhang, Guo-Wei Yang, Shuojin Yang), not 'Yingfei Deng'. arXiv page shows submission 25 Feb 2026 rather than 2026-03.

title: Structurally Aligned Subtask-Level Memory for Software Engineering Agents
summary: Argues instance-level memory (whole episode as the atomic unit) suffers a granularity mismatch, and aligns memory storage, retrieval and updating with the agent's functional decomposition into subtasks.
key_claims: Instance-level memory causes misguided retrieval when tasks share surface descriptions but need different reasoning at specific stages
+4.7 pp mean Pass@1 over the vanilla agent on SWE-bench Verified on average, +6.8 pp on Gemini 2.5 Pro
Gains grow with more interaction steps, i.e. memory helps most on long-horizon tasks
Consistently beats strong instance-level memory baselines across diverse backbones
Improves mean Pass@1 over the vanilla agent by +4.7 pp on average, e.g. +6.8 pp on Gemini 2.5 Pro, on SWE-bench Verified
Outperforms strong instance-level memory baselines across diverse backbones
Performance gains grow with more interaction steps
relevance: The clearest controlled result on write granularity for coding agents: subtask-level beats episode-level memory.

verification.notes: Shen et al., 25 Feb 2026. Abstract confirms +4.7pp mean Pass@1 and +6.8pp on Gemini 2.5 Pro, gains growing with interaction steps.

title: SWE-Exp: Experience-Driven Software Issue Resolution
summary: SWE-Exp distills concise, actionable experience from prior agent trajectories into a multi-faceted experience bank capturing both successful and failed repair attempts, at levels ranging from high-level problem comprehension to specific code changes.
key_claims: Current agents act as memoryless explorers, re-exploring failed trajectories across issues
73.0% Pass@1 on SWE-bench Verified with Claude 4 Sonnet
Storing failures as well as successes is explicitly required; failure experience prevents redundant exploration
Pass@1 resolution rate of 73.0% on SWE-Bench Verified with Claude 4 Sonnet
Characterizes current agents as memoryless explorers that treat each problem separately
relevance: Reference point for cross-issue experience memory on SWE-bench and for the success-plus-failure write policy.

verification.notes: Chen et al., 31 Jul 2025 (rev 2 Feb 2026). Abstract confirms 73.0% Pass@1 on SWE-bench Verified with Claude 4 Sonnet and the success+failure experience bank.

title: MemGovern: Enhancing Code Agents through Learning from Governed Human Experiences
summary: MemGovern governs raw GitHub issue-tracking data into agent-friendly 'experience cards' and adds an agentic experience-search strategy for logic-driven retrieval of human expertise, addressing the closed-world limitation of agents that fix bugs from local context only.
key_claims: Produces 135K governed experience cards from real GitHub issue data
Improves SWE-bench Verified resolution rate by 4.65% as a plug-in
Frames the problem as accessing open-world human experience rather than accumulating agent-only experience
relevance: Key counterpoint to self-generated memory: the highest-value memory for coding agents may be governed human experience, not agent trajectories.

verification.notes: arXiv:2601.06789. Abstract confirms 135K governed experience cards and +4.65% SWE-bench Verified resolution rate.

title: Exp-SWE-Agent: A Memory-Enhanced Coding Agent for Sequential Issue Resolution
summary: Augments Mini-SWE-Agent with a lightweight persistent memory module running a continuous retrieve-act-distill cycle that extracts structured factual and experiential knowledge from past issue-resolution trajectories for use as strategic hints.
key_claims: Pass rate rises from 42.7% to 47.5% on a sequential 8 x 25 subset of SWE-Bench Pro
Consistently reduces the number of interaction steps as well as improving accuracy
Submission to the FSE-AIWare 2026 MemComp challenge, evidence that cross-issue memory now has a dedicated competition track
Issue resolution rate rises from 42.7% to 47.5% on a sequential 8 x 25 subset of SWE-Bench Pro
Consistently reduces the number of interaction steps
relevance: Clean sequential-issue evidence with both accuracy and step-count effects; and evidence the SE community has institutionalised memory evaluation.

verification.notes: Could not verify. DOI 10.1145/3803437.3807663 returns 403 from ACM DL and the string 'Exp-SWE-Agent' returns zero hits on the open web (searches surface only the unrelated arXiv SWE-Exp paper). What IS confirmed: the FSE-AIWare 2026 MemComp challenge exists (mem-comp.github.io) and its evaluation is '200 instances: 8 projects x 25 instances per project' from SWE-Bench Pro, evaluated sequentially — matching the record's setup description. The 42.7%->47.5% figures and the paper's existence as a distinct publication remain unconfirmed; re-check against the FSE 2026 proceedings TOC before citing.

title: PROJECTMEM: A Local-First, Event-Sourced Memory and Judgment Layer for AI Coding Agents
summary: Local-first memory and judgment layer recording development as an append-only plain-text event log of typed events — issues, attempts, fixes, decisions, notes — deterministically projected into compact AI-readable summaries served over MCP. Beyond storage it adds a deterministic pre-action gate warning the agent before it repeats a previously failed fix or edits a known-fragile file, framed as Memory-as-Governance. Estimates 5,000-20,000 tokens per session spent reconstructing context; evaluated through a two-month self-study across 10 projects with 207 logged events.
key_claims: Estimates 5,000-20,000 tokens per session spent reconstructing project context
Append-only typed event log with deterministic projection into AI-readable summaries via MCP
Deterministic pre-action gate warns the agent before repeating a failed fix or editing a known-fragile file
Frames the contribution as Memory-as-Governance: memory that acts on the agent's next action
Two-month self-study across 10 projects, 207 logged events; runs fully offline as a provenance trail
Frames the design as Memory-as-Governance: memory acts on the agent's next action rather than just answering it
Ships as a three-dependency Python package with 14 MCP tools, 19 CLI commands, 37 automated tests
