title: Not All Skills Help: Measuring and Repairing Agent Knowledge (ASSAY)
summary: Separates skill generation (a creative act LLM judgment handles) from skill curation (which requires empirical evidence), computing per-skill causal attribution via randomized masking on a small development set and suppressing skills with negative predicted effect per test task.
key_claims: Skill libraries exhibit pervasive causal heterogeneity: individual skills help on some task types and hurt on others, and opposing effects cancel in aggregate so global curation cannot see them
DeepSeek-V3 reaches 69.3% task-goal completion on AppWorld's hardest split, a 47.4% relative improvement and SOTA over weight-tuned approaches
GPT-4.1 improves 8.7% relative on tau-bench retail without weight modification
Ablation attributes the dominant gain to per-task masking: the bottleneck is matching skills to tasks at inference, not removing bad skills globally
relevance: Shows memory utility is task-conditional, so a single global repo memory file is the wrong unit; admission must be per-task.

title: GRASP: Gated Regression-Aware Skill Proposer for Self-Improving LLM Agents
summary: GRASP treats agent improvement as a sequence of edits to a bounded skill library, admitting each candidate only if it produces net improvement on a balanced held-out probe under a hard regression budget.
key_claims: Lifts gpt-oss-120b from 40.6% to 88.8% on MedAgentBench, 21.0 points above the strongest of five self-improvement baselines, and improves every other base model by 17.2 to 40.3 points
Ablations attribute the gain to comparative proposal generation, the acceptance gate and the hard regression budget - skill writing without validation is no better than using no skills
Frozen libraries transfer across models and across benchmarks sharing a tool-calling convention, and degrade under interface mismatch
Mechanism helps where tasks recur with verifiable structure and is flat where the action space is open-ended
relevance: The clearest demonstration that the acceptance gate, not the authoring, is what makes self-written memory work - and that unvalidated writes are worthless.

verification.notes: Moll et al., 28 May 2026. Abstract contains 40.6%->88.8% on MedAgentBench, +21.0 points over best baseline, 17.2-40.3 points on other models, and the 'skill writing without validation is no better than no skills' ablation.

title: The Regression Tax: Decomposing Why Skills Help and Hurt LLM Agents
summary: Compares agents with and without skills across nearly 6,000 runs on two office-automation benchmarks and three model-harness stacks, distinguishing regressions (solved without skills, failed with) from residual failures.
key_claims: Best-performing skills win primarily by regressing less, not by gaining more
Three causes of regression: skill description osmosis (a skill changes behaviour merely by being in context even when never invoked), grounding displacement, verification displacement
Existing skills overemphasize procedural guidance - the stage least often responsible for failure - while under-supporting grounding and verification
Procedural skills should be evaluated by decomposing net effect into gains and regressions, not by aggregate improvement
relevance: Gives the evaluation protocol the memory literature lacks (gains vs regressions) and names osmosis - unused memory still changing behaviour.

title: SoK: Agentic Skills - Beyond Tool Use in LLM Agents
summary: Systematization of knowledge over the skill layer across its full lifecycle (discovery, practice, distillation, storage, composition, evaluation, update), with a seven-pattern system-level taxonomy and an orthogonal representation x scope taxonomy, plus a security analysis.
key_claims: Seven design patterns from metadata-driven progressive disclosure and executable code skills to self-evolving libraries and marketplace distribution
Representation x scope taxonomy: natural language, code, policy, hybrid across web, OS, software engineering, robotics
Case study of the ClawHavoc campaign in which nearly 1,200 malicious skills infiltrated a major agent marketplace, exfiltrating API keys, crypto wallets and browser credentials
Benchmark evidence that curated skills can substantially improve success rates while self-generated skills may degrade them
relevance: Only source here covering the supply-chain risk of shared procedural memory at ecosystem scale - a governance issue for skill marketplaces.

title: From Registry to Repository: How AI Agent Skills Are Written, Adapted, and Maintained
summary: First empirical study of AI agent skills as engineered artifacts, mining 18,463 skills from skills.sh and 23,199 personal-use skills from 5,876 GitHub repositories with 3,709 reuse links identified. Reuse is largely a one-time copy: most reused skills remain near-verbatim, 53% are never modified after adoption, and later maintenance is overwhelmingly additive. Customisation adapts skills to local environments while evolution accretes inline domain knowledge; the behavioural contract stays almost untouched.
key_claims: 18,463 registry skills and 23,199 personal-use skills from 5,876 repositories mined; 3,709 reuse links
53% of reused skills are never modified after adoption
Post-adoption maintenance is overwhelmingly additive
Six content categories from thematic analysis of 180 skills; six modification themes from coding 444 modifications
The behavioural contract of a skill (interaction, runtime monitoring, failure recovery) remains almost untouched across reuse
Reuse is largely a one-time copy: most reused skills remain near-verbatim and 53% are never modified after adoption
Subsequent local maintenance is overwhelmingly additive
Customisation primarily adapts skills to local environments; evolution accretes new inline domain knowledge
The behavioural contract - how a skill interacts with users, monitors runtime state, recovers from failures - remains almost untouched across modifications
Software Construction dominates the SWEBOK distribution with a long tail of specialised areas
relevance: Shows shared procedural memory propagates without review or adaptation — the ownership and provenance problem stated as a measurement.

title: A Self-Improving Coding Agent
authors_or_org: Maxime Robeyns, Martin Szummer, Laurence Aitchison
summary: Demonstrates that an agent system with basic coding tools can autonomously edit its own orchestration code and thereby improve its benchmark performance, a non-gradient learning mechanism driven by LLM reflection and code updates.
key_claims: Performance gains from 17% to 53% on a random subset of SWE-bench Verified
Additional gains on LiveCodeBench and synthetic agent benchmarks
Self-modification of the harness code itself, rather than of an external memory store, is the learning substrate
relevance: The limiting case of persistent memory for coding agents: the harness source code becomes the memory.

title: On the Structural Memory of LLM Agents
authors_or_org: Ruihong Zeng, Jinyuan Fang, Siwei Liu, Zaiqiao Meng
summary: Direct controlled comparison of four memory structures - chunks, knowledge triples, atomic facts, and summaries - plus mixed memory, crossed with three retrieval methods (single-step, reranking, iterative) over four tasks and six datasets.
key_claims: Different memory structures offer distinct advantages and should be tailored to the task; no single representation dominates
Mixed memory structures are remarkably resilient in noisy environments
Iterative retrieval consistently outperforms single-step retrieval and reranking across scenarios
relevance: The canonical representation-comparison study; its no-single-winner plus mixed-is-robust finding is the best available answer to markdown vs structured vs graph.

title: When Continual Learning Moves to Memory: A Study of Experience Reuse in LLM Agents
summary: Introduces a (k,v) framework disentangling how experience is represented from how it is organized for retrieval, and shows the stability-plasticity dilemma does not disappear with external memory but reappears at the memory-access level.
key_claims: Under a limited context window old and new experiences compete during retrieval, relocating the continual-learning bottleneck from parameter updates to memory access
Abstract procedural memories transfer more reliably than detailed trajectories
Negative transfer disproportionately harms the hard cases
Finer-grained memory organization is not universally beneficial: designs with strong forward transfer can simultaneously induce severe forgetting
relevance: The sharpest theoretical framing of the representation/organization trade-off, and the strongest statement that external memory reshapes rather than solves continual learning.

title: How Memory Management Impacts LLM Agents: An Empirical Study of Experience-Following Behavior
summary: Studies memory addition and deletion as the two fundamental operations and identifies the experience-following property: high input similarity to a retrieved record yields highly similar outputs.
key_claims: Two challenges follow from experience-following: error propagation, where inaccuracies compound over time, and misaligned experience replay, where seemingly correct executions give limited or misleading value
Controlled experiments show experience quality within the memory bank must be regulated
Future task evaluations can serve as free quality labels for stored memory
relevance: Explains mechanistically why unvalidated coding-agent memory degrades over time, and supplies a cheap validation signal (later outcomes as labels).

title: GitOfThoughts: Version-Controlled Reasoning and Agent Memory You Can Replay, Diff, and Merge
summary: Stores an agent's reasoning tree as a git repository - scored thoughts as commits, scores as notes, outcomes as tags, retrieval as git log - and uses it to run a pre-registered comparison of five memory stores across two benchmarks, two model sizes and repeated trials.
key_claims: Five memory stores compared: none, a markdown file, a vector database, a graph, and git
On new problems, memory does not improve accuracy - including one promising early result that did not replicate
Memory only helps once the problem is nearly identical to something in memory (cosine similarity above about 0.8); below that it does nothing
A model 4.5x larger still cannot extract a reusable method from a worked example; it only gets better at spotting near-copies
The only thing that reliably helped on new problems was self-consistency
Case for git as the store is auditability, history and mergeable memories at no cost to accuracy
relevance: The most direct head-to-head of markdown vs vector vs graph vs git memory, with a pre-registered null result that any SoA claim about memory must confront.

verification.notes: Shekar, H S, Krishnan; 12 Jun 2026. Abstract confirms five memory stores, pre-registered repeats, no gain on new problems, cosine ~0.8 threshold, 4.5x larger model still fails.

title: ByteRover: Agent-Native Memory Through LLM-Curated Hierarchical Context
summary: Inverts the memory pipeline so the same LLM that reasons also curates, structures and retrieves knowledge. Knowledge lives in a file-based hierarchical Context Tree (Domain/Topic/Subtopic/Entry) with explicit relations, provenance and an Adaptive Knowledge Lifecycle carrying importance scoring, maturity tiers and recency decay.
key_claims: Separating storage from reasoning causes semantic drift between what the agent meant to remember and what the pipeline captured
Five-tier progressive retrieval resolves most queries at sub-100 ms without LLM calls, escalating to agentic reasoning only for novel questions
SOTA on LoCoMo and competitive on LongMemEval with zero external infrastructure: no vector DB, no graph DB, no embedding service
All knowledge stored as human-readable markdown files on the local filesystem
relevance: The strongest result for human-readable markdown-in-repo memory beating vector/graph infrastructure, which is exactly the coding-harness form factor.

title: Evaluating Memory in LLM Agents via Incremental Multi-Turn Interactions (MemoryAgentBench)
authors_or_org: Yuanzhe Hu, Yu Wang, Julian McAuley
summary: Identifies four core competencies for memory agents from memory science - accurate retrieval, test-time learning, long-range understanding, selective forgetting - and builds a multi-turn benchmark covering all four, which no prior benchmark did.
key_claims: Four core memory competencies defined and operationalised
Existing benchmarks rely on limited context lengths or static long-context settings that do not reflect incremental accumulation
Current methods, from context-based and RAG systems to external-memory agents with tool integration, fall short of mastering all four
No prior benchmark covers all four memory competencies
Evaluated systems span context-only, RAG, external memory modules and tool-integrated agents; none masters all four competencies
relevance: Establishes selective forgetting as a measurable competency - the operation coding-agent memory stores most conspicuously lack.

title: MemoryArena: Benchmarking Agent Memory in Interdependent Multi-Session Agentic Tasks
summary: A unified evaluation gym for multi-session Memory-Agent-Environment loops, with human-crafted agentic tasks whose subtasks are explicitly interdependent: the agent must distil experience from earlier actions and feedback, then use it to solve later subtasks. Covers web navigation, preference-constrained planning, progressive information search and sequential formal reasoning.
key_claims: Agents with near-saturated performance on LoCoMo perform poorly in the interdependent agentic setting
Existing benchmarks assess memorization and action in isolation; MemoryArena couples them
Existing evaluations assess memorization and action in isolation, but in realistic settings they are tightly coupled
Agents with near-saturated performance on LoCoMo perform poorly in the agentic setting, exposing a gap in current memory evaluation
Covers web navigation, preference-constrained planning, progressive information search and sequential formal reasoning
relevance: Direct evidence that conversational memory scores do not transfer to agentic memory use — the transfer assumption implicit in applying LoCoMo-tuned memory to coding agents.

title: LongMemEval-V2: Evaluating Long-Term Agent Memory Toward Experienced Colleagues
summary: Benchmark of 451 manually curated questions over history trajectories of up to 500 trajectories and 115M tokens, testing five memory abilities for agents in customized environments: static state recall, dynamic state tracking, workflow knowledge, environment gotchas, premise awareness.
key_claims: AgentRunbook-C, which stores trajectories as files and invokes a coding agent to gather evidence in a sandbox, reaches 72.5% average accuracy
Strongest RAG baseline reaches 48.5% and the off-the-shelf coding-agent baseline 69.3%
Coding-agent-based memory methods advance the accuracy-latency Pareto frontier but carry high latency cost
Environment gotchas and workflow knowledge are named as first-class memory abilities distinct from user-history recall
relevance: Shows a coding agent operating over files is itself the best memory retrieval mechanism - a direct argument for file-based repo memory.

title: Continual Learning Bench: Evaluating Frontier AI Systems in Real-World Stateful Environments
summary: Expert-validated benchmark across six domains including software engineering, each designed so tasks share a learnable latent structure (e.g. codebase layout) that a stateful system can discover online but a stateless one cannot, with a gain metric isolating learning from prior capability.
key_claims: Agents frequently overfit to immediate observations or fail to reuse knowledge across instances
Dedicated memory systems do not fix this - naive in-context learning outperforms systems dedicated to memory management
First benchmark to isolate online learning from underlying model capability across diverse expert-validated real-world domains
Six expert-validated domains including software engineering; latent structure is learnable online
Agents overfit to immediate observations or fail to reuse knowledge across instances
Naive in-context learning outperforms systems dedicated to memory management
relevance: Blunt negative result on engineered memory systems versus plain ICL, with codebase layout as an explicit latent structure - central to the SoA gap analysis.

verification.notes: Asawa et al., 4 Jun 2026. Abstract confirms six domains incl. software engineering, gain metric, and 'naive ICL outperforms systems dedicated to memory management'.

title: From Recall to Forgetting: Benchmarking Long-Term Memory for Personalized Agents (Memora)
summary: A long-term memory benchmark spanning weeks-to-months of user conversation, evaluating remembering, reasoning and recommending, and introducing Forgetting-Aware Memory Accuracy (FAMA), a metric that penalizes reliance on obsolete or invalidated memory.
key_claims: Introduces FAMA, penalizing use of obsolete/invalidated memory
Four LLMs and six memory agents evaluated; frequent reuse of invalid memories and failure to reconcile evolving memories
Memory agents offer only marginal improvements over baselines
Evaluations of four LLMs and six memory agents reveal frequent reuse of invalid memories and failures to reconcile evolving memories
FAMA operationalises staleness as a first-class evaluation dimension
relevance: Gives the field its first staleness-penalizing metric; the direct analogue of what a repository memory must do when the code it described has changed.

verification.notes: Uddin et al., 21 Apr 2026. Abstract confirms remembering/reasoning/recommending and the FAMA metric penalising obsolete memory.

title: AgentPoison: Red-teaming LLM Agents via Poisoning Memory or Knowledge Bases
summary: The first backdoor attack targeting generic and RAG-based LLM agents by poisoning long-term memory or the knowledge base, formulating trigger generation as constrained optimization that maps triggered instances into a unique embedding region.
key_claims: Average attack success rate above 80% on three real-world agent types (autonomous driving, knowledge-intensive QA, healthcare EHRAgent)
Less than 1% impact on benign performance with a poison rate below 0.1%
Requires no additional model training or fine-tuning; triggers show transferability and stealth
Average attack success rate above 80% across three real-world agent types with less than 1% impact on benign performance
Poison rate below 0.1% suffices
Requires no additional model training or fine-tuning; triggers show strong transferability, in-context coherence and stealthiness
relevance: Establishes that a fraction of a percent of poisoned memory is enough for a durable backdoor — the scale argument for gating repository memory writes.

title: From Untrusted Input to Trusted Memory: A Systematic Study of Memory Poisoning Attacks in LLM Agents
summary: Systematic study of memory poisoning in LLM agents identifying four memory write channels and nine structural vulnerabilities across model capabilities, system prompt design and agent architecture, and deriving a taxonomy of six classes of memory poisoning attacks. Introduces MPBench and shows that agents designed to write and retrieve memory more aggressively are more exploitable, and that existing prompt-injection defenses do not cover memory poisoning.
key_claims: Four memory write channels and nine structural vulnerabilities identified
Taxonomy of six classes of memory poisoning attacks
Agents that write and retrieve memory more aggressively are more exploitable
Existing prompt injection defenses fail to cover memory poisoning
Releases MPBench for evaluating memory poisoning attacks
Four memory write channels and nine structural vulnerabilities enumerated
Agents designed to write and retrieve memory more aggressively are more exploitable
Existing prompt-injection defences fail to cover memory poisoning attacks
A single adversarial memory write can exert long-term influence over agent behaviour
Four memory write channels, nine structural vulnerabilities, six attack classes
relevance: Establishes an inverse relationship between memory-write aggressiveness and safety, which is the quantitative argument for conservative or human-gated write policies.

verification.notes: Dash et al., 3 Jun 2026. Abstract confirms four write channels, nine vulnerabilities, six attack classes, MPBench, and that prompt-injection defences do not cover memory poisoning.

title: Trojan Hippo: Weaponizing Agent Memory for Data Exfiltration
summary: Characterizes a class of persistent memory attacks in which a dormant payload is planted via a single untrusted tool call and activates only when the user later discusses sensitive topics, with a dynamic red-teaming evaluation framework across four memory backends.
key_claims: Up to 85-100% attack success rate against current frontier models from OpenAI and Google
Planted memories successfully activate even after 100 benign sessions
Four memory-system defences reduce attack success to as low as 0-5% but at widely varying utility cost
First capability-aware security/utility analysis for persistent memory systems
relevance: Demonstrates dormancy: poisoned memory survives 100 sessions, so periodic review of agent memory cannot be optional.

verification.notes: Das et al., 3 May 2026. Abstract confirms 85-100% ASR across four memory backends, activation after 100 benign sessions, defences to 0-5% at utility cost.

title: Beyond Similarity: Trustworthy Memory Search for Personal AI Agents (MemGate)
summary: Studies memory search as a trust boundary, evaluating A-Mem, Mem0 and MemOS plus a real personal-agent environment with persistent state and tool use, then inserts a 9M-parameter gate between the vector store and the backbone LLM to turn raw similarity search into task-conditioned memory admission.
key_claims: Long-term memory is a durable control channel that can reshape how agents interpret tasks and execute actions
Threats enabled by similarity-only retrieval: cross-domain leakage, sycophancy, tool-call drift, memory-induced jailbreaks
MemGate is 9M parameters and 35.1MB, requires no LLM modification, memory-database rewriting or inference-time LLM judge
Reduces memory-induced threats across memory frameworks and backbones while preserving utility
relevance: Shifts the safety problem to the read path: what gets retrieved is as much a control decision as what gets written.

title: FSFM: A Biologically-Inspired Framework for Selective Forgetting of Agent Memory
summary: Argues a well-designed forgetting mechanism is as crucial as remembering, and establishes a taxonomy of forgetting mechanisms: passive decay-based, active deletion-based, safety-triggered, and adaptive reinforcement-based.
key_claims: Forgetting delivers benefits across three dimensions: efficiency via pruning, quality via updating outdated preferences and context, security via active forgetting of malicious or sensitive input
Reported improvements: access efficiency +8.49%, content signal-to-noise ratio +29.2%, 100% elimination of the studied security risks
Connects forgetting to ethical and regulatory compliance requirements
relevance: The most explicit treatment of forgetting as a governance control, including safety-triggered deletion - absent from every coding-harness memory design surveyed.

verification.notes: Gu et al., Apr 2026. Abstract contains access efficiency +8.49%, content quality +29.2% SNR, 100% elimination of security risks. (Body tables show the 100% figure; the two percentage figures appear in the abstract only.)

title: Evaluating Very Long-Term Conversational Memory of LLM Agents
authors_or_org: Adyasha Maharana, Dong-Ho Lee, Sergey Tulyakov, Mohit Bansal, Francesco Barbieri, Yuwei Fang
summary: Introduces LoCoMo, a dataset of very long-term conversations generated by an LLM-agent/human pipeline grounded in personas and temporal event graphs, then verified and edited by human annotators. Each conversation averages 300 turns and 9K tokens over up to 35 sessions. The benchmark measures long-term memory via question answering, event summarization, and multi-modal dialogue generation.
key_claims: LoCoMo conversations average 300 turns and 9K tokens over up to 35 sessions
LLMs struggle with long-range temporal and causal dynamics in lengthy conversations
Long-context LLMs and RAG improve results but remain substantially below human performance
relevance: The de facto default memory benchmark that almost every memory system reports on; entirely conversational and non-SE, so it anchors the SoA claim that memory evaluation grew up outside software engineering.

verification.notes: Maharana et al., 27 Feb 2024. Abstract: 300 turns / 9K tokens avg / up to 35 sessions.

title: LongMemEval: Benchmarking Chat Assistants on Long-Term Interactive Memory
authors_or_org: Di Wu, Hongwei Wang, Wenhao Yu, Yuwei Zhang, Kai-Wei Chang, Dong Yu
summary: LongMemEval evaluates five core long-term memory abilities of chat assistants: information extraction, multi-session reasoning, temporal reasoning, knowledge updates, and abstention. It contains 500 curated questions embedded in freely scalable user-assistant chat histories, and decomposes memory design into indexing, retrieval and reading stages.
key_claims: 500 curated questions across five memory abilities, with scalable chat-history length
Commercial chat assistants and long-context LLMs show a 30% accuracy drop on memorizing information across sustained interactions
Session decomposition, fact-augmented key expansion and time-aware query expansion improve both recall and downstream QA
relevance: Second pillar of the conversational memory benchmark canon and the one that most cleanly separates write/index/read stages — a decomposition SE memory work has not yet adopted.

title: MemBench: Towards More Comprehensive Evaluation on the Memory of LLM-based Agents
authors_or_org: Haoran Tan, Zeyu Zhang, Chen Ma, Xu Chen, Quanyu Dai, Zhenhua Dong
summary: Builds a dataset distinguishing factual memory from reflective memory and participation from observation as interaction scenarios, then evaluates memory capability along effectiveness, efficiency and capacity axes.
key_claims: Separates factual vs reflective memory levels and participation vs observation scenarios
Reports effectiveness, efficiency and capacity rather than accuracy alone
relevance: One of the few benchmarks that treats memory capacity and efficiency as first-class metrics, which is the axis SE work needs for cost accounting.

title: MemGym: a Long-Horizon Memory Environment for LLM Agents
summary: MemGym unifies existing agent gyms and memory-grounded pipelines behind a single memory-reasoning interface, spanning five tracks across four agentic regimes: tool-use dialogue (tau2-bench), deep-research search (MEMGYM-DR), coding (SWE-Gym and MEMGYM-CODEQA), and computer use (WebArena-Infinity). It reports memory-isolated scores that decouple memory quality from reasoning, retrieval and tool-use ability.
key_claims: Reports memory-isolated scores so memory strategies can be ranked without reasoning/tool-use confounders
Includes a coding regime built on SWE-Gym plus a synthetic MEMGYM-CODEQA pipeline
Trains MemRM, a Qwen3-1.7B QLoRA reward model, to score compression quality as a fast scalar substitute for full Docker rollouts
relevance: The closest thing to an SE-inclusive memory benchmark: it is the only one found that puts a coding regime behind a memory-isolated scoring protocol, i.e. where memory can be varied independently of the model.

verification.notes: Xu et al., 20 May 2026. Abstract confirms memory-isolated scores, SWE-Gym coding track, MEMGYM-CODEQA, MemRM (Qwen3-1.7B QLoRA).

title: MemoryRewardBench: Benchmarking Reward Models for Long-Term Memory Management in Large Language Models
summary: First benchmark for whether reward models can reliably judge long-term memory management. Covers long-context comprehension and long-form generation, with 10 settings of differing memory-management patterns and contexts from 8K to 128K tokens, evaluating 13 reward models.
key_claims: 10 distinct settings with different memory management patterns; context length 8K-128K tokens
13 cutting-edge reward models evaluated; open-source/proprietary gap is shrinking and newer generations beat predecessors regardless of parameter count
Exposes fundamental limitations of current RMs in judging memory management
relevance: Memory is increasingly optimized with learned rewards; this shows the judge itself is unvalidated, which undermines the whole RL-for-memory line including SWE-MeM-style coding agents.

verification.notes: Tang et al., 17 Jan 2026. Abstract confirms 10 settings, 8K-128K context, 13 reward models.

title: MemOps: Benchmarking Lifecycle Memory Operations in Long-Horizon Conversations
summary: Argues that memory is a lifecycle of explicit operations — remembering, forgetting, updating, reflecting and their compositions — rather than a static fact collection. Each memory event is a structured trace specifying trigger, target, scope, state transition and supporting evidence, with gold operation traces and six categories of operation-level probes.
key_claims: Final-answer accuracy conflates heterogeneous causes of failure and can credit correct answers that rest on inconsistent or unsafe memory states
Session-level retrieval outperforms turn-level retrieval
Long-context models are notably weak at reconstructing ordered memory-state trajectories
Evaluated across long-context, retrieval-based, parametric and managed-memory systems; none is uniformly reliable
relevance: The single strongest methodological argument in the track: outcome accuracy masks memory failure, so any SE memory claim resting on resolve-rate alone is under-evidenced.

verification.notes: Hao et al., 14 Jul 2026. Abstract confirms lifecycle operations, gold traces, 'can credit correct answers despite reliance on inconsistent or unsafe memory states', session- vs turn-level retrieval.

title: Beyond a Million Tokens: Benchmarking and Enhancing Long-Term Memory in LLMs (BEAM / LIGHT)
summary: Generates coherent, topically diverse conversations up to 10M tokens with probing questions, yielding BEAM: 100 conversations and 2,000 validated questions. LIGHT equips LLMs with episodic memory, short-term working memory and a scratchpad of salient facts.
key_claims: BEAM: 100 conversations, 2,000 validated questions, conversations up to 10M tokens
Even 1M-token-context LLMs, with and without retrieval augmentation, degrade as dialogues lengthen
LIGHT improves 3.5%-12.69% over the strongest baselines depending on backbone
relevance: Pushes horizon far past LoCoMo/LongMemEval and demonstrates that long context alone does not substitute for memory — the key premise behind repository memory for SE agents.

title: StreamBench: Towards Benchmarking Continuous Improvement of Language Agents
summary: Benchmarks continuous improvement of LLM agents over an input-feedback sequence, simulating an online learning environment where the agent receives a feedback stream and must iteratively improve, with baselines for streaming strategies.
key_claims: Existing benchmarks evaluate innate capability, not improvement over time
Provides simple baselines and an analysis of which components drive successful streaming strategies
relevance: The earliest of the streaming/self-improvement benchmarks and the ancestor of Evo-Memory, CL-Bench and AgentCL; establishes the sequential-task protocol that SWE-Bench-CL later ports to code.

title: Evo-Memory: Benchmarking LLM Agent Test-time Learning with Self-Evolving Memory
summary: A streaming benchmark and framework for self-evolving memory: datasets are structured into sequential task streams so the agent must search, adapt and evolve memory after each interaction. Unifies over ten memory modules across 10 multi-turn goal-oriented and single-turn reasoning/QA datasets.
key_claims: Over ten representative memory modules re-implemented and compared on a common streaming protocol
10 datasets spanning multi-turn goal-oriented and single-turn reasoning/QA
Provides ExpRAG baseline for experience reuse and ReMem action-think-memory refine pipeline
relevance: One of the few harnesses where memory modules are swapped under a fixed model and task stream — the independence property SE evaluations still lack.

title: EvoMemBench: Benchmarking Agent Memory from a Self-Evolving Perspective
summary: Organizes agent memory along two axes — memory scope (in-episode vs cross-episode) and memory content (knowledge-oriented vs execution-oriented) — and compares 15 memory methods against strong long-context baselines under a standardized protocol.
key_claims: 15 representative memory methods compared under one protocol
Long-context baselines remain highly competitive; memory helps most when current context is insufficient or tasks are difficult

No single memory form works consistently across settings: retrieval wins on knowledge-intensive tasks, procedural/long-term memory on execution-oriented tasks when stored experience matches task structure
relevance: Supplies the sharpest 'memory does not always help' controlled result and the in-episode vs cross-episode axis that maps directly onto session vs cross-session repository memory.

title: AMA-Bench: Evaluating Long-Horizon Memory for Agentic Applications
summary: Evaluates memory over real agent-environment interaction trajectories (states, actions, observations, tool outputs) rather than dialogue, combining real trajectories with expert-curated QA and synthetic trajectories that scale to arbitrary horizons.
key_claims: Existing memory benchmarks are dialogue-centric while real agent memory consists of interaction trajectories
Existing memory systems fail to capture causal and objective information and over-rely on lossy similarity retrieval
AMA-Agent (causality graph + tool-augmented retrieval) reaches 57.22% accuracy, 11.16% above the strongest baseline
relevance: Trajectory-shaped memory is exactly what a coding agent accumulates; AMA-Bench shows similarity retrieval over trajectories is the dominant failure.

title: MEMPROBE: Probing Long-Term Agent Memory via Hidden User-State Recovery
summary: Argues long-term memory should be audited as a post-interaction artifact: after ordinary assistance, what structured user state can be reconstructed from the memory left behind? Spans 50 simulated users with 31 hidden dimensions each (1,550 recovery targets) across 5 memory systems, under full-store and top-k access.
key_claims: 50 simulated users, 31 hidden dimensions each, 1,550 recovery targets, 5 memory systems
Task completion nearly saturates even for a memoryless baseline, while category-balanced memory recovery stays around 0.6 and drops further under top-k retrieval
Successful assistance and recoverable memory behave as distinct capabilities
relevance: Strongest single number for 'task success does not measure memory': a memoryless baseline nearly saturates task completion while memory recovery sits at ~0.6.

title: Episodic Memories Generation and Evaluation Benchmark for Large Language Models
authors_or_org: Alexis Huet, Zied Ben Houidi, Dario Rossi
summary: Builds a cognitively grounded representation of episodic events (temporal and spatial context, entities, descriptions) and synthesizes a contamination-free episodic memory benchmark with open code and datasets.
key_claims: Benchmark is synthesized to be free from contamination

State-of-the-art models including GPT-4, Claude variants, Llama 3.1 and o1-mini struggle, particularly with multiple related events and complex spatio-temporal relations, even at 10k-100k token contexts
relevance: One of the very few memory benchmarks with an explicit contamination argument — a property none of the SE memory proxies can currently claim.

title: AgentCL: Toward Rigorous Evaluation of Continual Learning in Language Agents
summary: Constructs compositional task streams where earlier sub-solutions, evidence or workflows are intentionally reusable later, contrasted with naive streams where reuse is not guaranteed, and measures transfer gains. MemProbe stores interactions, insights and skills while filtering unreliable experiences during consolidation.
key_claims: Naive task streams offer limited ability to distinguish memory designs; controlled compositional streams distinguish plasticity more clearly
Naive and held-out settings often yield limited gains and can expose memory-induced degradation
Evaluated across coding, deep research, and language understanding/reasoning
relevance: Shows that how a task stream is constructed determines whether memory looks useful at all — a direct methodological warning for sequential SWE-bench protocols.

title: HaluMem: Evaluating Hallucinations in Memory Systems of Agents
summary: First operation-level hallucination benchmark for memory systems, defining memory extraction, memory updating and memory QA as separate evaluation tasks so hallucinations can be localized to a stage. Datasets HaluMem-Medium and HaluMem-Long each contain ~15k memory points and ~3.5k questions.
key_claims: ~15k memory points and ~3.5k multi-type questions per dataset; average 1.5k and 2.6k dialogue turns per user, contexts exceeding 1M tokens
Memory systems generate and accumulate hallucinations during extraction and updating, which then propagate into question answering
Hallucination classes: fabrication, errors, conflicts, omissions
relevance: Establishes hallucinated memory as a measurable, stage-localizable failure — the write-time analogue of a coding agent recording a wrong architectural fact.

title: MemTrace: Probing What Final Accuracy Misses in Long-Term Memory
summary: Makes the knowledge point — a single typed fact about the user — the unit of measurement instead of the question row, probing each fact along memory age, question type (current state / earlier state / trajectory of change) and evidence condition (present / missing / contradicted by false premise).
key_claims: 13 memory-system configurations across four paradigms evaluated
Similar pooled accuracy hides different failures: recovering current and earlier states does not imply tracking how a fact changed, and safe abstention does not imply correcting a false premise
The dominant bottleneck is evidence use, not retrieval: when systems fail, the evidence was retrievable 10 times more often than it was missing
relevance: The 10x evidence-use-vs-retrieval figure reframes where memory effort should go, and contradicts retrieval-centric repo-memory designs.

title: DynamicMem: A Long-Horizon Memory Benchmark in Real-World Settings
summary: Synthesizes 15 months of multi-app activity per user (averaging 2.2M tokens and 1,772 grounded events across 16 applications) with an implicit, drifting profile that must be inferred; evaluation runs at five quarterly checkpoints as history grows.
key_claims: 2.2M tokens and 1,772 grounded events per user across 16 applications, 15 months, five quarterly checkpoints
Profile reconstruction degrades with history length while service-task accuracy stays flat, despite both drawing on the same memory
No system both keeps facts that stay true and replaces facts that change
Over 93% of failures trace to what memory retrieves, not to the answering model
relevance: The scale-with-history degradation result is precisely the regime a long-lived repository memory enters; the 93% retrieval-attribution number is a key SoA statistic.

title: STALE: Can LLM Agents Know When Their Memories Are No Longer Valid?
summary: Isolates Implicit Conflict — a later observation invalidating an earlier memory without explicit negation — with 400 expert-validated conflict scenarios and 1,200 evaluation queries over 100+ everyday topics, contexts up to 150K tokens, probing State Resolution, Premise Resistance and Implicit Policy Adaptation.
key_claims: 400 expert-validated conflict scenarios, 1,200 queries, contexts up to 150K tokens
Best evaluated model reaches only 55.2% overall accuracy
Pervasive gap between retrieving updated evidence and acting on it; models accept outdated assumptions embedded in queries
relevance: The canonical stale-memory benchmark. Implicit conflict is exactly what happens when a refactor silently invalidates a remembered fact about the codebase.

verification.notes: Chao et al., 7 May 2026. Abstract confirms 400 expert-validated conflict scenarios, 1,200 queries, up to 150K tokens, and best model only 55.2% overall.

title: A-TMA: Decoupling State-Aware Memory Failures in Long-Term Agent Memory
summary: Names ghost memory: old, current and transition facts coexisting in the bank, mixed at retrieval, misleading the answer model. Proposes a state-aware overlay keeping superseded and transition records with explicit labels, and builds LTP (LoCoMo Temporal Plus), a conflict-heavy benchmark.
key_claims: On LTP, Graphiti+ATMA improves conflict accuracy by 0.240 absolute over Graphiti
On LoCoMo, Graphiti+ATMA raises temporal F1 from 0.0295 to 0.1705
Calls for decoupled evaluation of bank, retrieval and answer-level failures since final QA accuracy hides where ghost memory occurs
relevance: Quantifies how weak temporal handling is in a deployed graph memory (temporal F1 of 0.0295) — a caution for anyone assuming graph memory solves repo evolution.

title: MemConflict: Evaluating Long-Term Memory Systems Under Memory Conflicts
summary: A diagnostic framework treating memory validity as a query-conditioned fitness-for-use problem, formalizing dynamic, static and conditional conflicts over temporal validity, factual correctness and contextual applicability, with injected semantically similar distractors.
key_claims: Six representative long-term memory systems evaluated with both black-box answer scoring and white-box retrieval/ranking analysis
Answer correctness often diverges from memory retrieval and ranking quality
Longer histories, distractors, implicit queries and larger conflict distances all degrade performance
relevance: Contradiction handling is the least-studied memory failure in SE contexts; this supplies both a taxonomy and the divergence-from-answer-accuracy evidence.

title: Your Agents Are Aging Too: Agent Lifespan Engineering for Deployed Systems (AgingBench)
summary: A longitudinal reliability benchmark organizing agent aging into compression aging, interference aging, revision aging and maintenance aging, using temporal dependency graphs and paired counterfactual probes to produce diagnostic profiles for write, retrieval and utilization stages.
key_claims: 7 scenarios, 14 models, multiple memory policies, ~400 runs spanning 8-200 sessions
Agent aging is not one-dimensional: behavioral tests can stay clean while factual precision decays; derived-state tracking can collapse sharply within a single model
The same wrong answer can require different repairs depending on the diagnostic profile
relevance: Frames reliability as a lifespan property of the whole harness rather than a day-one model property — the exact framing the SoA paper needs for long-lived repo agents.

title: When Stored Evidence Stops Being Usable: Scale-Conditioned Evaluation of Agent Memory
summary: An evaluation protocol under evidence-preserving growth: task evidence is held fixed per query while irrelevant sessions accumulate. Reports budget-compliant reliability, tail memory-call burden, failure-regime decomposition, and the usable-scale boundary where reliability falls below target.
key_claims: On LongMemEval, HippoRAG stays within a two-call budget but loses 16-20 percentage points of budget-compliant reliability as irrelevant sessions are added
LiCoMemory's failures depend strongly on the agent: Qwen3-8B exceeds the call budget while Qwen3-32B and Qwen3-235B remain reliable
Scalable-memory claims must be conditional on agent, interface, scale range and interaction budget
relevance: Quantifies memory bloat: adding only irrelevant material costs 16-20 points. Directly applicable to a repo memory that grows with every issue.

title: MemDelta: Controlled Baselines and Hidden Confounds in Agent Memory Evaluation
summary: A controlled protocol varying one component at a time on LongMemEval-S (500 questions, 50+ sessions, three model families) to separate memory-method effects from language-model, embedding-model and retrieval-pipeline effects.
key_claims: Verbatim RAG matches full-context GPT-4o-mini (47.2% vs 49.8%, p = 0.34), but the ranking reverses across models: Gemini gains +14pp from full context while Sonnet gains +31pp from RAG (partly because it refuses 63% of full-context queries)
Swapping only the embedding model shifts accuracy by +6.2pp (p = 0.004); Mem0 beats MiniLM-RAG by +11pp but loses to cloud-RAG by 1.2pp
Agent self-memory (42%) underperforms basic retrieval (47%)
On 2 of 6 question types Mem0 matches cloud RAG (72.7% vs 73.9%, p = 1.0) at 50x the cost
relevance: The scaffold-effect result for memory: reported memory gains are frequently embedding-model or model-family effects. Pairs with `scaffold-effect-coding-agents-2026` in the harness store.

verification.notes: Kuan Wang, 29 Jun 2026. Abstract contains 47.2 vs 49.8 (p=0.34), +6.2pp embedding swap (p=0.004), self-memory 42% vs retrieval 47%, Mem0 72.7 vs 73.9 (p=1.0) at 50x cost. All four record claims verbatim.

title: Are We Ready For An Agent-Native Memory System?
summary: A systematic experimental study of agent memory from a data-management perspective, decomposing memory into representation/storage, extraction, retrieval/routing and maintenance, and evaluating 12 memory systems plus two reference baselines across five workloads spanning 11 datasets.
key_claims: 12 representative memory systems and two baselines across five benchmark workloads / 11 datasets
No single architecture dominates; effectiveness depends on how well memory structure aligns with the workload bottleneck
Localized maintenance is more cost-efficient than global reorganization
relevance: The broadest head-to-head comparison found, and its no-dominant-architecture conclusion is the cleanest summary of the evaluation state of the art.

title: TwinMem-Agent: Episodic and Semantic Memory for Repository-Level Program Repair
venue: FSE 2026 (Proceedings of the 34th ACM International Conference on the Foundations of Software Engineering)
summary: Studies the sequential maintenance regime on a stratified 8 x 25 subset of SWE-Bench Pro (eight projects, twenty-five instances each), running instances in commit-time order within each project so later repairs draw on earlier trajectories. Pairs a test-patch-validate loop with episodic memory (grounded demonstrations) and semantic memory (LLM-distilled notes), compacting each trajectory under a fixed budget.
key_claims: 89.1% Pass@1 versus 60.0% for mini-swe-agent baseline on the same Dockerized instances with DeepSeek-V3.2
Roughly 18x lower average inference cost ($0.0044 vs $0.0798)
Removing the memory module reduces Pass@1 by 8 pp and reproduction success rate (RSR) by 12 pp on 25 Ansible instances
The larger RSR drop indicates cross-issue experience most directly benefits bug reproduction
relevance: The clearest existing measurement of repository memory across sessions: SWE-Bench Pro instances replayed in commit order with memory carried forward, plus a memory ablation.

verification.notes: Checked as an extra (memo quotes 'MemComp 89.1 vs 60.0'). DOI 10.1145/3803437.3807664 returns 403 from ACM DL and 'TwinMem-Agent' returns zero open-web hits. The MemComp challenge and its 8x25 SWE-Bench Pro sequential setup are confirmed; the 89.1% vs 60.0%, ~18x cost and -8pp ablation figures are not independently verifiable. Same caveat as exp-swe-agent-memcomp-2026.

title: SWE Context Bench: A Benchmark for Context Learning in Coding
summary: Explicitly evaluates whether coding agents reuse experience across related problems: 1,100 base tasks plus 376 related tasks derived from real dependency and reference relationships among GitHub issues and pull requests, grouped by shared context across 51 repositories and 9 languages.
key_claims: 1,100 base tasks and 376 related tasks across 51 repositories and 9 programming languages
Accurately summarized and retrieved prior experience significantly improves resolution accuracy and reduces runtime and token cost, particularly on harder tasks
Unfiltered or incorrectly selected context provides limited or negative benefits
relevance: The one SE benchmark built around genuinely related task pairs, so context/memory can be varied while the task set is held fixed; also supplies the SE-side 'wrong context hurts' result.

title: ExpeRepair: Dual-Memory Enhanced LLM-Based Repository-Level Program Repair
venue: Proceedings of the ACM on Software Engineering
summary: A dual-memory repair framework inspired by human cognition: an episodic memory storing concrete repair demonstrations and a semantic memory encoding abstract reflective insights, combined through dynamic prompt composition at inference time.
key_claims: pass@1 of 60.3% on SWE-Bench Lite and 74.6% on SWE-Bench Verified
Best performance among evaluated open-source methods
Continuously learns from historical repair experiences via dual-channel knowledge accumulation
relevance: Establishes the episodic/semantic split that TwinMem-Agent later carries into the sequential SWE-Bench Pro setting; a peer-reviewed SE anchor for the dual-memory design.

title: Learning to Commit: Generating Organic Pull Requests via Online Repository Memory
summary: Under a strict chronological repository split, the agent blindly attempts each historical issue, compares its prediction against the oracle diff, and distils the gap into a growing set of skills capturing coding style, internal API usage and architectural invariants. Evaluation is on genuinely future merged PRs unseen during skill building.
key_claims: Argues agents fail on organicity — ignoring project conventions, duplicating internal APIs, violating implicit architectural constraints — not functional correctness
A latest-snapshot view shows the final state but not the repository-specific change patterns that produced it
Evaluated on held-out future PRs across functional correctness, code-style consistency, internal API reuse rate and modified-region plausibility
relevance: Best example of contamination-aware SE memory evaluation: a strict chronological split with held-out future PRs, which is how cross-session repo memory should be measured.

title: Learning When to Remember: Risk-Sensitive Contextual Bandits for Abstention-Aware Memory Retrieval in LLM-Based Coding Agents
summary: Reframes issue-memory use as a selective, risk-sensitive control problem: a bandit controller chooses among no memory, top-resolution injection, multi-candidate summary, high-precision or high-recall retrieval, abstention, or asking for feedback, with false-positive memory injection penalized more strongly than missed reuse.
key_claims: Superficial similarity in stack traces, terminal errors, paths or configuration symptoms leads to unsafe memory injection
62.5% offline replay success rate at 0.0% false-positive rate (strongest non-oracle result in the reported artifacts)
60.5% proxy success with 0.0% false positives and 331.466 microseconds p95 decision latency in a bounded 200-case validation
relevance: Makes abstention a first-class memory action for coding agents and names the SE-specific over-retrieval hazard (stack-trace surface similarity). Note: smoke-scale artifacts, so treat numbers as indicative.

verification.notes: Mehmet Iscan, 30 Apr 2026. Abstract: 62.5% offline replay success at 0.0% FP; 60.5% proxy success, 0.0% FP, 331.466 microseconds p95.

title: Why Git Is the Memory Solution for the Agentic Development Lifecycle
summary: Argues agent memory should be git-bound, inheriting ground truth from commits, freshness from rebuild, verification from the merge, and containment from review, rather than built as tiered stores and model-judged admission machinery. Solves seed supply as an eight-corpus retrieval study under pre-registered ship discipline (five imported ranking mechanisms rejected, two kept, best configuration ~0.31 pooled MRR, roughly 60x the raw-transcript grep floor). Finds single-shot retrieval scores only 0.07-0.20 answer-sufficiency on real developer questions and that ungated episode injection measurably degrades good answers; a router dispatching breadth, pointed lookups and rationale separately reaches 0.83 sufficiency on a ~50k-LOC production system at 382-980 tokens per question.
key_claims: Git-bound memory inherits ground truth from commits, freshness from rebuild, verification from merge, containment from review
Best retrieval configuration ~0.31 pooled MRR, about 60x the raw-transcript grep floor and 15x an honest parsed-turn floor
Single-shot retrieval yields only 0.07-0.20 answer-sufficiency on real developer questions
Ungated episode injection measurably degrades otherwise good answers
Routed system reaches 0.83 answer sufficiency at 382-980 tokens per question, three orders of magnitude below the recorded history
Ground truth mined from commit-session links rather than annotation, so results replicate on any user's history at zero labeling cost

Eight-corpus retrieval study under pre-registered ship discipline: five imported ranking mechanisms rejected, two kept, best configuration ~0.31 pooled MRR (~60x the raw-transcript grep floor, ~15x an honest parsed-turn floor)
Single-shot retrieval scores only 0.07-0.20 answer-sufficiency on real developer questions, and ungated episode injection measurably degrades good answers
Routed decision synthesis reaches 0.83 sufficiency on a ~50k-LOC production system at 382-980 tokens per question
Ground truth is mined from commit-session links rather than annotated, so results replicate on any user's own history at zero labeling cost
relevance: The strongest argument that existing human review machinery (code review, merge) is already the validation layer for agent memory — and the ungated-injection-degrades-answers result is a direct hit on unsupervised memory write.

verification.notes: Frank Guo, 15 Jul 2026. Abstract confirms ~0.31 pooled MRR, 0.07-0.20 single-shot answer sufficiency, ungated episode injection degrading good answers, 0.83 routed sufficiency, 382-980 tokens/question.

title: Context Rot in AI-Assisted Software Development: Repurposing Documentation Consistency for AI Configuration Artifacts
summary: Names 'context rot' — the staleness of persistent AI configuration files (CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, .cursorrules) as software evolves — and argues that decades of documentation-consistency tooling (README, comment, API, architecture and installation checkers) is the immediate starting point for detecting it. As preliminary evidence, applying an existing README/wiki consistency checker to a statistically representative sample of 356 repositories identifies stale code element references in 23.0% of repositories.
key_claims: Coins 'context rot' for staleness of AI configuration artifacts as code evolves
Statistically representative sample of 356 repositories
An existing README/wiki consistency checker finds stale code element references in 23.0% of repositories
Proposes a roadmap mapping documentation-consistency approaches onto context-file problems
Applying an existing README/wiki consistency checker to a statistically representative sample of 356 repositories identifies stale code element references in 23.0% of repositories
Existing documentation-consistency tools can already surface context rot
Connects AI configuration artifacts to prior work on README, comment, API doc, architecture and installation-instruction consistency
relevance: The key bridge between classical SE documentation research and agent memory governance: repo memory needs expiry and consistency checking, and existing tooling can already partly supply it.

verification.notes: Treude & Baltes, 8 Jun 2026. Abstract confirms 356-repository representative sample and 23.0% stale code element references. (/abs render was empty; /html served the page.)

title: Why Does CLAUDE.md Keep Growing? Catastrophic Remembering in Agentic Coding
summary: Traces unbounded growth of agentic coding READMEs to imperfect recall: appending an instruction is cheap, but once its rationale is gone, deleting it without risking a regression costs O(2^|D|) in a prompt of |D| instructions. Names the resulting divergence catastrophic remembering, the inverse of catastrophic forgetting.
key_claims: Characterized across 247,694 instruction lifetimes in 1,867 repositories
Agentic prompts more than triple over their lifetime (+226%), gaining +4.9 net instructions every commit
The older an instruction gets, the less likely it is to be deleted (log-hazard -0.032/commit)
Comments encoding latent reasoning remove 99.3% of excess instructions in inverted-IFEval worlds (+211.3% to +1.4%) and improve real-world agentic instruction-following by up to 23.1% on WildIFEval
relevance: The memory-bloat failure mode measured at scale on real repositories, with a mechanism (lost rationale makes deletion unsafe) and a cheap mitigation (rationale comments).

title: Configuration Smells in AGENTS.md Files: Common Mistakes in Configuring Coding Agents
authors_or_org: Helio Victor F. dos Santos, Vitor Costa, Joao Eduardo Montandon, Luciana Lourdes Silva, Marco Tulio Valente
summary: First catalog of smells for coding-agent configuration files, derived from a grey literature review plus repository mining, with automated detection heuristics for six smells. Analysis of 100 popular open-source repositories containing AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md finds smells widespread: Lint Leakage 62%, Context Bloat 42%, Skill Leakage 35%, with Context Bloat, Skill Leakage and Conflicting Instructions frequently co-occurring.
key_claims: Six configuration smells identified with automated detection heuristics
100 popular open-source repositories analyzed
Lint Leakage affects 62% of files, Context Bloat 42%, Skill Leakage 35%
Context Bloat, Skill Leakage and Conflicting Instructions frequently co-occur
relevance: Establishes that human-authored agent memory has its own quality-decay taxonomy, giving artifact mining a concrete measurable target for 'is this memory any good'.

verification.notes: dos Santos et al., 14 Jun 2026. Abstract: 100 repos, Lint Leakage 62%, Context Bloat 42%, Skill Leakage 35%, co-occurrence.

title: When Retrieval Hurts Code Completion: A Diagnostic Study of Stale Repository Context
summary: A controlled diagnostic study on 17 production-helper signature changes from five Python repositories, comparing current-only, stale-only, no-retrieval and mixed retrieval conditions under prompts that hide commit freshness and expected current signatures.
key_claims: Stale-only retrieval induces stale helper references on 15/17 samples for Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct and 13/17 for gpt-4.1-mini, i.e. 88.2 and 76.5 percentage-point increases over current-only retrieval
No retrieval produces zero stale references but only 1/17 passing completions
The two models share 75.0% Jaccard overlap among stale-triggering samples; adding valid current evidence largely rescues stale-only failures
Temporal validity of retrieved repository context is a distinct diagnostic variable for Code RAG robustness
relevance: Shows stale repository memory is not benign noise: it actively biases the model toward obsolete repository state. Directly links context rot to wrong code.

verification.notes: Weng et al. Abstract confirms 17-sample set, 15/17 (Qwen2.5-Coder-7B) and 13/17 (gpt-4.1-mini), +88.2 and +76.5 pp over current-only retrieval.

title: Failure-Gated Hierarchical Memory: Preventing Memory Pollution in Long-Horizon LLM Agents via Critic-Guided Write Control
summary: Three-tier memory (working, episodic buffer, procedural long-term) with a dedicated Failure Critic — a LoRA-tuned Llama-3-8B trained on hard-negative candidates from failure trajectories — gating all writes from the episodic buffer to procedural long-term memory with APPROVE / REJECT_REDUNDANT / REJECT_CONFLICT verdicts. Salvageable rejects go through a reflective abstraction loop, and sandbox consistency verification replays historical failures with the candidate injected. On ALFWorld (670 scenarios, 5-round reset), WebShop (200 tasks) and MemoryAgentBench FactConsolidation, it cuts long-term memory pollution from 38% (naive LLM summarization) to 9% with only 4pp success-rate degradation over 5 rounds versus 20+ points for baselines.
key_claims: Long-term memory pollution rate reduced from 38% (naive LLM summarization) to 9%
Task success degradation of only 4 percentage points over 5 rounds versus 20+ points for baselines
Evaluated on ALFWorld (670 scenarios), WebShop (200 tasks), MemoryAgentBench FactConsolidation
Critic is a LoRA-tuned Llama-3-8B issuing APPROVE / REJECT_REDUNDANT / REJECT_CONFLICT verdicts
Proposes LTM Pollution Rate (LPR) as a memory-quality metric
Reduces long-term memory pollution rate from 38% (naive LLM summarization) to 9%
Proposes LTM Pollution Rate (LPR) as a memory-quality metric complementing task-level metrics
Evaluated on ALFWorld (670 scenarios), WebShop (200 tasks) and MemoryAgentBench FactConsolidation
relevance: Introduces an explicit approve/reject verdict vocabulary and a pollution-rate metric — the machine analogue of a human memory-review workflow, with the review cost automated away.

title: Memory Injection Attacks on LLM Agents via Query-Only Interaction (MINJA)
authors_or_org: Shen Dong, Shaochen Xu, Pengfei He, Yige Li, Jiliang Tang, Tianming Liu, Hui Liu, Zhen Xiang
summary: The canonical memory-injection attack: the adversary never touches the memory bank directly, injecting malicious records purely through queries and observed outputs. Bridging steps link victim queries to malicious reasoning, and a progressive shortening strategy removes the indication prompt so the record is retrieved for later victim queries.
key_claims: No assumption of direct memory-bank access; injection occurs through ordinary query interaction
Effective across diverse agents with minimal execution requirements, so any user can influence agent memory
A follow-up evaluation reports MINJA achieving over 95% injection success and 70% attack success under idealized conditions (arXiv:2601.05504)
relevance: The reference threat model for writable agent memory and the baseline nearly every later defence measures against.

title: Memory Poisoning Attack and Defense on Memory Based LLM-Agents
summary: Systematically varies initial memory state, number of indication prompts and retrieval parameters to test how robust MINJA-style attacks are outside idealized conditions, on EHR agents using MIMIC-III data across GPT-4o-mini, Gemini-2.0-Flash and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. Proposes I/O moderation with composite trust scoring and memory sanitization with temporal decay.
key_claims: MINJA reported at over 95% injection success and 70% attack success under idealized conditions
Realistic conditions with pre-existing legitimate memories dramatically reduce attack effectiveness
Effective memory sanitization needs careful trust-threshold calibration to avoid both blocking all entries and missing subtle attacks
relevance: The rare replication study; shows headline poisoning rates are strongly setup-dependent, which should temper how the SoA paper reports attack success rates.

title: MemoryGraft: Persistent Compromise of LLM Agents via Poisoned Experience Retrieval
summary: An indirect injection attack that implants malicious successful experiences into long-term memory, exploiting the agent's semantic imitation heuristic — its tendency to replicate patterns from retrieved successful tasks — rather than jailbreaking it.
key_claims: Validated on MetaGPT's DataInterpreter agent with GPT-4o
A small number of poisoned records accounts for a large fraction of retrieved experiences on benign workloads
Turns experience-based self-improvement into a vector for stealthy, durable behavioural drift across sessions
relevance: Attacks a code-writing agent's experience store specifically, so it is the closest security result to SE experience memory (SWE-Exp, ExpeRepair, MemOp).

title: Poison Once, Exploit Forever: Environment-Injected Memory Poisoning Attacks on Web Agents
summary: eTAMP is the first attack achieving cross-session, cross-site compromise with no direct memory access: a single contaminated observation (e.g. a manipulated product page) silently poisons memory and activates during later tasks on different sites, bypassing permission-based defences.
key_claims: Attack success up to 32.5% on GPT-5-mini, 23.4% on GPT-5.2, and 19.5% on GPT-OSS-120B on (Visual)WebArena
Frustration Exploitation: agents under environmental stress are up to 8x more susceptible when struggling with dropped clicks or garbled text
More capable models are not more secure — GPT-5.2 shows substantial vulnerability despite superior task performance
relevance: Contamination through ordinary observation alone is the realistic threat model for a coding agent that reads issues, docs and dependency pages; the Frustration Exploitation finding is novel and important.

title: Hidden in Memory: Sleeper Memory Poisoning in LLM Agents
summary: Studies delayed attacks where an adversary manipulates external context — a document, webpage, or repository — to cause the assistant to store a fabricated memory that lies dormant and re-emerges across later conversations. Evaluates the full write-retrieve-use pipeline.
key_claims: Poisoned memories were added up to 99.8% of the time on GPT-5.5 and 95% on Kimi-K2.6
Among successful retrievals, poisoned memories cause attacker-intended agentic actions in 60-89% of evaluations across models
Explicitly names repositories as an injection channel
relevance: Highest reported write-success rates for poisoned memory on frontier assistants, with repositories named as a vector — directly relevant to agents reading untrusted code.

title: Injection-Execution Dissociation: A Mechanistic Evaluation of Persistent Memory Attacks and Defenses in Stateful LLM Agents
summary: Shows prompt-injection success and tool-execution success are separable safety properties: defences that block injection do not necessarily block execution and vice versa. A 5,040-run factorial experiment across nine open-source models evaluates six defences at four architectural layers against delayed-trigger attacks persisting across sessions via RAG retrieval.
key_claims: Malicious instructions are stored at rates exceeding 97.5%, yet downstream execution ranges from 0% to 95% with no correlation to storage rate
5,040-run factorial experiment, nine models, N=40 per condition; frontier evaluation over 21 models and 3 providers
Only Memory Sandbox, a tool-layer defence structurally isolating recalled memory from executable context, reduces attack success to 0% for eight of nine models
Vendor-correlated patterns: Anthropic blocks predominantly at injection, OpenAI at execution; stored-but-dormant payloads are a compositional supply-chain risk in shared-memory deployments
relevance: Reframes the defence target: preventing storage is insufficient, authority boundaries between memory ingestion and action execution must be structurally enforced.

title: Bad Memory: Evaluating Prompt Injection Risks from Memory in Agentic Systems
summary: Studies prompt injection in memory-based agentic systems using a sandboxed synthetic workspace, evaluating Anthropic Claude Code and OpenAI Codex across four models. Although it is difficult to make an agent overwrite its own memory files using untrusted external content, payloads already planted in those files successfully attack current and future sessions, with attack success and payload persistence varying substantially across systems, models, adversarial goals and multi-session attack sequences.
key_claims: Two agentic systems (Claude Code, OpenAI Codex) across four models (Claude Haiku 4.5, Claude Opus 4.7, GPT-5.2, GPT-5.5)
Making an agent overwrite its own memory files using untrusted external content is difficult
Payloads already planted in memory files successfully attack current and future sessions
Attack success and payload persistence vary substantially across systems, models, goals and multi-session sequences
Persistent memory changes the threat model for prompt injection; defenses must protect memory updates without removing useful adaptation
It is difficult to make an agent overwrite its own memory files using untrusted external content
Attack success and payload persistence vary substantially across systems, models, adversarial goals and multi-session sequences
relevance: The direct security case for gating writes to repo memory files in coding agents specifically — and evidence that the write path, not the read path, is the defensible chokepoint.

title: What If Prompt Injection Never Left? Rethinking Agent Security through Cross-Session Stored Prompt Injection
summary: Introduces Cross-Session Stored Prompt Injection, modelled on stored XSS: persistent state (memories, filesystems, tools, long-lived context artifacts) extends prompt injection across time and space. Provides a lifecycle formalization, a taxonomy of persistence channels and incorporation mechanisms, and a sandbox toolkit.
key_claims: The fundamental challenge is not filtering untrusted inputs but governing how external information acquires authority as it crosses persistent system boundaries
Calls for a shift from interaction-centric to state-centric security
Taxonomy of persistence channels covering memories, filesystems and tool state
relevance: Gives the SoA paper a clean conceptual frame — memory as an authority boundary — that unifies the poisoning, compaction and governance-decay results.

title: From Prompt Injection to Persistent Control: Defending Agentic Workspaces Against Trojan Backdoors (ClawTrojan / DASGuard)
summary: A benchmark for multi-step trojan attacks in local agentic harnesses where an injection embedded in a file or tool output is read, stored in workspace state, and executed later — no single step looking malicious. DASGuard scans control-like text in sensitive local files, traces its origin, and removes control content lacking a trusted source.
key_claims: 95.5% attack success rate in an OpenClaw-style simulated workspace with GPT-5.4, while existing single-turn prompt-injection attacks produce near-zero ASR on the same model
Existing defences inspect each step in isolation and miss the earlier write that plants the backdoor
DASGuard combines runtime blocking with sanitized commits to the workspace
relevance: Quantifies the gap between single-turn and multi-step-through-memory threat models in a local coding workspace (near-0% vs 95.5%), and the defence is provenance-based.

verification.notes: Paper exists (arXiv:2605.31042, Tan, Dou, Yang, Hu, Cheng, Li, Wen) and the 95.5% ASR with GPT-5.4 in an OpenClaw-style workspace vs near-zero single-turn ASR is verbatim in the abstract. Title is wrong: 'Defending Agentic Workspaces Against Trojan Backdoors', not 'Defending Agentic Harness'. The third key_claim ('DASGuard combines runtime blocking with sanitized commits') is not what the abstract says — DASGuard 'scans control-like text in sensitive local files, traces its origin, and removes control content that does not originate from a trusted source'.

title: Securing LLM-Agent Long-Term Memory Against Poisoning: Non-Malleable, Origin-Bound Authority with Machine-Checked Guarantees (TMA-NM)
summary: Shows both content-based and lineage-based memory-authority signals are malleable: an attacker can launder an untrusted origin through the agent's own summarization, a trusted-tool echo, or manufactured corroboration. Proves a machine-checked separation theorem and builds non-malleable information-flow control for agent memory.
key_claims: Existing defences reach up to 68% laundering attack success, exactly where the theory predicts failure
TMA-NM reaches 0% attack success on both direct and laundering attacks across all eight frontier models and channels, at full legitimate utility
Write-time origin binding is proven necessary; content- or lineage-based defences are unsound under laundering
Releases benchmark, harness and machine-checked TLA+ models

title: Sleep-time agents (Letta)
summary: Letta's sleep-time agents ('dreaming') are background subagents that review recent conversations, consolidate lessons and update memory without interrupting active work. They run after a configurable number of agent steps or when the context window is compacted, and commit to MemFS, a git-backed memory filesystem.

title: letta-code: stateful agents with memory, identity, and the ability to learn and adapt
summary: Letta Code is a coding agent built on Letta's stateful-agent stack: memory blocks in the system prompt, skill learning, and sleep-time compute. All context including memory blocks is tracked via git in MemFS, synced to a local .agents/ directory or a user-designated GitHub repository.

Apache-2.0 licensed

title: LangMem SDK for agent long-term memory
summary: LangMem (launched 2025-02-18) helps agents learn through long-term memory across three types: semantic (facts), procedural (learned rules saved as updated prompt instructions), and episodic (past interactions distilled into few-shot examples).

'LangMem doesn't yet support opinionated utilities for episodic memory'

Procedural memory is implemented as prompt optimization based on performance feedback

title: Long-term memory (LangChain/LangGraph docs)
summary: LangGraph stores long-term memories as JSON documents in a store, organized by namespace (folder) and key (file name), read with runtime.store.get() and written with store.put(). Backends include InMemoryStore (development only) and PostgreSQL, with Redis and MongoDB via integrations; semantic search across namespaces is supported.

InMemoryStore is development-only; PostgreSQL is the production-ready backend, with Redis and MongoDB via integrations

Semantic search across namespaces uses vector similarity plus content filters

title: Memory organization in AgentCore Memory
summary: AgentCore Memory organizes short-term memory by sessionId and actorId (events created with CreateEvent) and long-term memory by hierarchical namespaces of the form /strategy/{memoryStrategyId}/actor/{actorId}/session/{sessionId}/, with granularity from per-session up to global.

Namespace template: /strategy/{memoryStrategyId}/actor/{actorId}/session/{sessionId}/ with trailing slashes to avoid prefix collisions
Granularity levels run from per-session through actor-level and strategy-level to global (/)
IAM policies can restrict memory access using bedrock-agentcore:namespace and namespacePath condition keys
relevance: The only memory platform surveyed that expresses memory scope as an IAM-enforceable path — the cloud-governance answer to 'who can read this memory'.

title: Memory (Agent Development Kit)
summary: ADK's MemoryService exposes add_session_to_memory, add_events_to_memory, add_memory and search_memory. Implementations are InMemoryMemoryService (non-persistent, keyword matching), VertexAiMemoryBankService (managed, LLM-extracted semantic memories) and VertexAiRagMemoryService (vector similarity over raw transcripts).

Writes are performed by application code via callbacks or manual invocation, typically after session completion
Memory is scoped by app_name and user_id
Agents retrieve memories with the load_memory and preload_memory tools or ToolContext.search_memory()
relevance: Makes the extraction-vs-retrieval split explicit as a product choice (Memory Bank vs RAG service), a distinction most vendor docs blur.

title: Step 4: Memory & Persistence (Microsoft Agent Framework)
summary: Microsoft Agent Framework separates chat history providers (InMemoryChatHistoryProvider and custom stores) from context providers, which run before_run() to inject instructions and after_run() to extract and store information. Mem0 is available as a first-party context provider.
key_claims: Context providers implement before_run() to extend instructions and after_run() to extract and store information, maintaining per-session state
Chat history providers store conversation history; agents default to InMemoryChatHistoryProvider or the underlying service's storage
Multiple providers can be composed (e.g. history store + Mem0ContextProvider + audit store); only one should set load_messages=True
Mem0 integration ships as Mem0Provider in both Python and .NET

title: Supermemory documentation (introduction)
summary: Supermemory positions itself as 'context infrastructure for AI agents', offered as a hosted API, as a plugin/MCP integration for Claude and coding agents, or self-hosted locally. The introduction page does not document memory types, retention, benchmarks, or who writes memories.
key_claims: Three deployment modes: cloud API, plugin/MCP integration for Claude and coding agents, self-hosted local
The introduction page discloses no memory types, retention policy, benchmark numbers or write policy
relevance: Representative of the thin-disclosure end of the memory-platform market: positioning without a documented memory model.

title: Knowledge Graph Memory Server (@modelcontextprotocol/server-memory)
summary: The reference MCP memory server stores a local knowledge graph of entities (name, type, observations), relations (directed, active voice) and observations (atomic facts), persisted as JSONL at a path set by MEMORY_FILE_PATH. Eight tools cover create/add/delete/read/search.
key_claims: Data model: entities with unique name, type and observation list; directed relations stored in active voice; atomic string observations
Eight tools: create entities and relations, add observations, delete entities/observations/relations, read the full graph, search nodes
Persisted as JSONL; storage path configurable via MEMORY_FILE_PATH; deployable via Docker or NPX
Supports live update notifications to subscribed clients on mutation
relevance: The de-facto default when a developer adds 'memory' to any MCP-capable coding agent — worth noting that it has no expiry, validation or approval whatsoever.

title: Linux Foundation Announces the Formation of the Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF), Anchored by New Project Contributions Including Model Context Protocol (MCP), goose and AGENTS.md
summary: Press release (2025-12-09) announcing the Agentic AI Foundation under the Linux Foundation, with MCP contributed by Anthropic, goose by Block and AGENTS.md by OpenAI, and platinum members including AWS, Anthropic, Block, Bloomberg, Cloudflare, Google, Microsoft and OpenAI.
