MCP is stated to have over 10,000 published servers
AGENTS.md was contributed to the foundation by OpenAI; MCP by Anthropic; goose by Block
Platinum members: AWS, Anthropic, Block, Bloomberg, Cloudflare, Google, Microsoft, OpenAI
relevance: Dates the neutral-governance moment for the repo-memory file format and supplies the only adoption number (60,000 repos) available for AGENTS.md.

title: On the Impact of AGENTS.md Files on the Efficiency of AI Coding Agents
authors_or_org: Jai Lal Lulla, Seyedmoein Mohsenimofidi, Matthias Galster, Jie M. Zhang, Sebastian Baltes, Christoph Treude
summary: Runs AI coding agents on GitHub pull requests with and without an AGENTS.md file, across 10 repositories and 124 pull requests, measuring wall-clock runtime and token consumption. Presence of AGENTS.md is associated with 28.64% lower median runtime and 16.58% lower output token consumption, with comparable task completion behaviour.
key_claims: 10 repositories, 124 pull requests, two conditions (with/without AGENTS.md)
Median runtime lower by 28.64% with AGENTS.md
Output token consumption lower by 16.58% with AGENTS.md
Task completion behaviour comparable between conditions
relevance: The efficiency counterpart to Gloaguen: human-written context files may not raise success rates but can cut runtime and output tokens. The two results are about different outcome variables and are often conflated.

verification.notes: Lulla, Mohsenimofidi, Galster, Zhang, Baltes, Treude; 28 Jan 2026. Abstract: 10 repos, 124 PRs, lower median runtime (delta 28.64%) and reduced OUTPUT token consumption (delta 16.58%). Record correctly says output tokens, not total.

title: Do Context Files Help Coding Agents? A Two-Agent Ablation Study on Real Repositories
summary: Controlled ablation of context-injection strategy across two frontier agents (Claude Code and Codex), 17 real tasks from 3 repositories, and 288 evaluated runs with gold-test evaluation. Context strategy does not measurably move correctness on either agent, bounded to <=10-15pp by equivalence testing. Failure-mode triage attributes failures to implementation skill rather than missing repository knowledge; a manipulation probe shows the real AGENTS.md never converts a near-miss to a pass.
key_claims: 288 evaluated runs, 17 tasks, 3 repositories, 2 agents (Claude Code, Codex)
Context strategy does not measurably move correctness; equivalence bound <=10-15pp
Failures are implementation-skill failures (feature design, pattern selection, wiring), not missing repository knowledge
Manipulation probe: the real AGENTS.md never converts a near-miss to a pass on either agent
Borderline task difficulty is agent-specific (Spearman rho=0.75), a candidate explanation for contradictory prior findings
relevance: Explains *why* context files fail to lift correctness and offers a methodological account of the field's contradictions — essential for ranking open questions by answerability.

verification.notes: Prakhar Khatri, 28 Jul 2026. Abstract: 288 runs, 17 tasks, 3 repos, <=10-15pp equivalence bound, manipulation probe, Spearman rho=0.75.

title: Guardrails Beat Guidance: A Large-Scale Study of Rules, Skills, and Persistent Configuration for Coding Agents
authors_or_org: Xing Zhang, Guanghui Wang, Yanwei Cui, Wei Qiu, Ziyuan Li, Bing Zhu, Peiyang He
summary: First large-scale controlled study of agent rule files (CLAUDE.md, .cursorrules, skills, plugin manifests, persona definitions): 679 rule files with 25,532 rules scraped from GitHub and over 5,000 Claude Code runs with Claude Opus 4.6 on SWE-bench Verified. Random rules improve performance as much as expert-curated ones (both +13.8pp on a discriminative subset). Rule polarity separates beneficial from harmful: every individually beneficial rule is a negative constraint, every individually harmful one a positive directive.
key_claims: 679 rule files, 25,532 rules mined from GitHub; >5,000 Claude Code runs with Opus 4.6 on SWE-bench Verified
Random rules and expert-curated rules both give +13.8pp on a discriminative SWE-bench Verified subset
Gains are largely content-independent (random, shuffled, mismatched-domain, unconverted-format all match curated) — a context-priming mechanism
Every individually beneficial rule is a negative constraint; every individually harmful one is a positive directive
Pass rates remain stable across rule counts from 0 to 50 — harm does not visibly accumulate in ensemble
relevance: The sharpest challenge to human curation as a value-add: if random rules match expert rules, the measured benefit of human-written memory is priming, not knowledge. Directly reframes 'who should write memory'.

verification.notes: Zhang et al., 13 Apr 2026. Abstract: 679 rule files / 25,532 rules / >5,000 Claude Code runs on SWE-bench Verified; both random and curated +13.8pp on a discriminative subset; polarity finding; stable 0-50 rules.

title: Instruction Adherence in Coding Agent Configuration Files: A Factorial Study of Four File-Structure Variables
summary: Factorial study of four structural variables of coding-agent configuration files (file size, instruction position, file architecture, contradictions in adjacent files), measuring compliance with a trivial target annotation across 1,650 Claude Code CLI sessions and 16,050 function-level observations on two TypeScript codebases. None of the four variables or three two-way interactions produces a detectable contrast after multiple-testing correction; size and conflict nulls carry affirmative-null Bayes factors (BF10 0.05-0.10). The largest effect is within-session decay: roughly 5.6% lower odds of compliance per additional generated function (OR = 0.944).
key_claims: 1,650 Claude Code CLI sessions, 16,050 function-level observations, two TypeScript codebases, five coding tasks
No detectable contrast from file size, instruction position, file architecture, or adjacent-file contradictions
Affirmative-null Bayes factors BF10 between 0.05 and 0.10 for size and conflict
Within-session compliance decay: ~5.6% lower odds per additional generated function (OR = 0.944), non-monotonic
Decay reproduces on a second TypeScript codebase and on Opus 4.6 at matched configuration
relevance: Shows the practitioner folklore about how to *structure* human-written memory is unsupported, while the real threat to adherence is temporal decay inside a session — a harness problem, not an authoring problem.

verification.notes: Damon McMillan, 11 May 2026. Abstract: 1,650 sessions / 16,050 observations, BF10 0.05-0.10 for size and conflict, 5.6% lower odds per generated function (OR=0.944).

title: Configuring Agentic AI Coding Tools: An Exploratory Study
authors_or_org: Matthias Galster, Seyedmoein Mohsenimofidi, Sebastian Baltes, Christoph Treude
venue: AIware 2026 (Proc. 3rd ACM Int. Conf. on AI-Powered Software)
summary: Peer-reviewed venue version of the harness-configuration study. Identifies eight configuration mechanisms for agentic AI coding tools spanning static context to executable and external integrations, and examines adoption across 2,853 GitHub repositories covering Claude Code, GitHub Copilot, Cursor, Gemini and Codex. Context Files dominate and are often the sole mechanism; Skills and Subagents are rarely adopted and Skills mostly carry static instructions rather than executable scripts.

2,853 GitHub repositories analyzed
Context Files dominate and are often the only configuration mechanism in a repository; AGENTS.md emerging as interoperable standard
Few repositories adopt Skills or Subagents; Skills are predominantly static instructions
Claude Code users employ the broadest range of mechanisms

title: A Dataset of Agentic AI Coding Tool Configurations
authors_or_org: Matthias Galster, Seyedmoein Mohsenimofidi, Sebastian Baltes, Christoph Treude
venue: AIware 2026 (Proc. 3rd ACM Int. Conf. on AI-Powered Software)
summary: Curated dataset of repository-level agent configuration artifacts mined from GitHub. From 40,585 actively maintained repositories, 36,710 were classified as engineered software projects; the released dataset covers 4,738 repositories across five tools and eight configuration mechanisms, with 15,591 configuration artifacts, the full content of 18,167 configuration files, and 148,519 AI-co-authored commits. 4,738 repositories, five tools, eight configuration mechanisms in the released dataset
15,591 configuration artifacts and 18,167 configuration file contents collected
148,519 AI-co-authored commits included
Dataset and pipeline on Zenodo under CC BY 4.0

title: Beyond the Prompt: An Empirical Study of Cursor Rules
venue: MSR 2026 (23rd Int. Conf. on Mining Software Repositories)
summary: First large-scale characterization of developer-authored persistent directives for AI coding assistants. Qualitative analysis of 401 open-source repositories containing cursor rules yields a taxonomy of essential project context organized into five high-level themes: Conventions, Guidelines, Project Information, LLM Directives, and Examples. Also explores how this context varies across project types and programming languages.
key_claims: 401 open-source repositories with cursor rules analyzed qualitatively
Five-theme taxonomy: Conventions, Guidelines, Project Information, LLM Directives, Examples
Context content varies across project type and programming language
relevance: The first content taxonomy of human-written agent rules, and the reference point for later Cursor-rules mining studies.

title: A Study of Cursorrules Files in GitHub Open Source Projects
summary: Empirical study of 12,110+ .cursorrules files from 11,427 GitHub repositories characterizing distribution, evolution and maintenance, plus qualitative analysis of a random sample of 65 prompt files with a 65-code codebook. Adoption emerged rapidly from mid-2024 and is concentrated in small-scale, low-activity, single-maintainer repositories. Content is dominated by code quality and engineering practices, project structure and maintainability; security content appears less frequently. Themes carry over from legacy .cursorrules to current .mdc files.
key_claims: 12,110+ .cursorrules files from 11,427 GitHub repositories
Adoption emerged rapidly from mid-2024
Adoption concentrated in small-scale, low-activity, single-maintainer repositories, suggesting toy projects rather than professional development
Content dominated by code quality, engineering practice, project structure and maintainability; security rare
Thematic continuity between legacy .cursorrules and current .mdc files
relevance: Calibrates who the authors of agent memory actually are — mostly solo maintainers of small projects — which bounds claims about team-level memory governance in the wild.

title: Rule Taxonomy and Evolution in AI IDEs: A Mining and Survey Study
summary: Mixed-methods study mining 83 open-source projects for 7,310 rules and triangulating with 99 practitioner survey responses. Yields a 5-primary / 25-secondary category taxonomy. Practitioners rate architectural constraints as highly important while repository rule files are dominated by low-level workflow and formatting constraints. Analysis of 1,540 rule evolution events shows frequent updates, driven in repositories by context expansions (29.17%) and enrichments (26.59%); surveyed developers say they mostly edit rules to correct AI errors (77.78%), typically by adding negative constraints. Compliance assessment of 160 rule evolution events shows average artifact compliance rising 22.99pp, from 49.14% to 72.13%, after an update.
key_claims: 83 projects mined, 7,310 rules extracted, 99 practitioners surveyed
Taxonomy of 5 primary and 25 secondary rule categories
1,540 rule evolution events analyzed; context expansions 29.17%, enrichments 26.59%
77.78% of surveyed developers modify rules primarily to correct AI errors, usually by adding negative constraints
Artifact compliance rises from 49.14% to 72.13% (+22.99pp) after a rule update, over 160 evolution events
relevance: The single best triangulated evidence on the human-write loop: developers write memory reactively, after observing agent failure, and the negative constraints they add measurably raise compliance.

title: Context Engineering for AI Agents in Open-Source Software
authors_or_org: Seyedmoein Mohsenimofidi, Matthias Galster, Sebastian Baltes, Christoph Treude
venue: MSR 2026 (23rd Int. Conf. on Mining Software Repositories)
summary: Preliminary study of AI context file adoption in 466 open-source projects, analysing what information developers provide in AGENTS.md, how they present it, and how the files evolve. Finds no established content structure and wide variation in presentation mode (descriptive, prescriptive, prohibitive, explanatory, conditional), with a commit-level analysis giving first insight into context evolution.
key_claims: 466 open-source projects analyzed for AGENTS.md adoption
No established content structure has emerged
Context is provided in five presentation modes: descriptive, prescriptive, prohibitive, explanatory, conditional
Commit-level analysis gives first insights into how provided context evolves
relevance: Introduces the prescriptive/prohibitive distinction that Guardrails-Beat-Guidance later shows is the polarity axis separating helpful from harmful human-written memory.

title: Evolution Context Gap: An Empirical Study of Agent Manifests
summary: Content analysis of 80 real-world agent manifests across five agent types using a six-category taxonomy and a three-model LLM classifier with majority-vote consensus. Workflow & Process dominates (present in 96.2% of manifests, 43.5% mean character fraction), while evolution context is largely absent: 73.8% of manifests contain no evolution content and none references Lehman's laws. One significant project-level correlation: manifests in more law-conformant projects contain more coding-style guidance (rho = 0.431, p = 0.040, n=23).
key_claims: 80 manifests across five agent types, six-category taxonomy, three-model majority-vote classifier
Workflow & Process present in 96.2% of manifests, 43.5% mean character fraction
73.8% of manifests contain no evolution content; none reference Lehman's laws of software evolution
Coding-style guidance correlates with project law-conformance (rho = 0.431, p = 0.040, n=23)
relevance: Identifies a specific blind spot in human-written memory — nothing about how the system changes over time — which is precisely the knowledge agents cannot recover from a code snapshot.

title: How Do Developers Maintain and Evolve Their Agents' Instructions? An Empirical Study
summary: Registered-report style plan for a large-scale mining study of Agent Context File (ACF) evolution. Proposes to classify ACF changes with a taxonomy grounded in software maintenance theory, analyse how change types associate with code quality outcomes, and examine temporal patterns across the development lifecycle, combining repositories containing ACFs with agent-generated commits. Motivated explicitly by governance, traceability, and control over agent behaviour.
key_claims: Frames Agent Context Files as maintained artifacts and proposes a maintenance-theory taxonomy for their changes
Plans commit-level reconstruction of ACF evolution linked to agent-generated commits
Plans statistical analysis of association between ACF change categories and code quality metrics
States governance, traceability and control over agent behaviour as the motivating problem
relevance: The explicit research design for the artifact-mining path on 'when is memory written and does it help', which is the more answerable half of the open questions.

verification.notes: Voria, Cannavale, De Lucia, Kashiwa, Catolino, Palomba. It is a registered report (Context/Objective/Method, no results); record correctly phrases every claim as 'plans'.

title: ContextCov: Deriving and Enforcing Executable Constraints from Agent Instruction Files
summary: Compiles natural-language instructions from AGENTS.md into executable guardrails: static AST queries for code patterns, runtime shell shims intercepting prohibited commands, and architectural validators for structural rules. Acting as a continuous automated reviewer, it returns reproducible violation traces so the agent can self-correct before non-compliant changes are finalized. On SWE-bench Lite (12 repositories, 300 tasks) it reaches 88.3% constraint compliance vs 67.0% prompt-only and 50.3% LLM-reflection, at 3.4x lower feedback cost while preserving functional correctness.
key_claims: 88.3% constraint compliance vs 67.0% prompt-only and 50.3% LLM-reflection baselines
3.4x lower feedback cost than baselines
Evaluated on SWE-bench Lite, 12 repositories, 300 tasks
Passive natural-language instructions are frequently violated due to context saturation or conflicting local context
relevance: Demonstrates the strongest available validation policy for human-written memory: compile it into executable checks rather than trusting the agent to read and obey it.

title: A Deterministic Control Plane for LLM Coding Agents
summary: Prevalence study of 10,008 public GitHub repositories (n=6,145 agent config files) showing agent configurations propagate as undeclared shared components: 10.1% of tracked paths are SHA-256 exact duplicates across independent repositories (fork-adjusted), with 75.5% of clone pairs crossing organisational boundaries. Configurations are rarely revised (58% single-commit; 0.4 vs 0.6 commits/month age-normalised against CI/CD workflows) and rarely declare permission boundaries (<1% of agent configs vs 33% of Actions workflows). Proposes Rel(AI)Build, a deterministic control plane treating agent definitions as a managed supply chain with content addressing, HMAC-stamped lockfiles, hash-chained audit logs, tiered permissions and prompt-drift detection.
key_claims: 10,008 public repositories, 6,145 agent config files analyzed
10.1% of tracked config paths are SHA-256 exact duplicates across independent repositories; 75.5% of clone pairs cross organisational boundaries
58% of agent configurations are single-commit; 0.4 vs 0.6 commits/month versus CI/CD workflows
<1% of agent configs declare permission boundaries vs 33% of GitHub Actions workflows (n=31 true positives)
Proposes deterministic, tool-agnostic governance of the configuration layer rather than LLM orchestration
relevance: The clearest accountability evidence: agent memory files are copied across organisations, almost never revised, and almost never scoped — an unowned, unversioned supply chain.

title: SkillReducer: Optimizing LLM Agent Skills for Token Efficiency
summary: Large-scale study of 55,315 publicly available agent skills finds systemic inefficiency: 26.4% lack routing descriptions, over 60% of body content is non-actionable, and reference files can inject tens of thousands of tokens per invocation. SkillReducer compresses routing descriptions and restructures skill bodies with progressive disclosure, achieving 48% description compression and 39% body compression while improving functional quality by 2.8% on 600 skills and SkillsBench.
key_claims: 55,315 public agent skills analyzed
26.4% of skills lack routing descriptions entirely; over 60% of body content is non-actionable
48% description compression and 39% body compression with +2.8% functional quality
Mean retention 0.965 across five models from four families
A 'less-is-more' effect: removing non-essential content reduces context-window distraction
relevance: Quantifies the bloat problem in community-authored procedural memory — the same Context Bloat smell the AGENTS.md literature reports, at marketplace scale.

title: Agent Skills in the Wild: An Empirical Study of Security Vulnerabilities at Scale
summary: First large-scale security analysis of the agent-skill ecosystem: 42,447 skills collected from two marketplaces, 31,132 analysed with SkillScan (static analysis plus LLM semantic classification). 26.1% of skills contain at least one vulnerability across 14 patterns in four categories; data exfiltration (13.3%) and privilege escalation (11.8%) are most prevalent and 5.2% show high-severity patterns suggesting malicious intent. Skills bundling executable scripts are 2.12x more likely to be vulnerable (OR=2.12, p<0.001).

26.1% of skills contain at least one vulnerability across 14 patterns
Data exfiltration 13.3%, privilege escalation 11.8%, high-severity malicious-intent patterns 5.2%
Script-bundling skills 2.12x more likely to contain vulnerabilities (OR=2.12, p<0.001)
Detection methodology achieves 86.7% precision and 82.5% recall
Skills execute with implicit trust and minimal vetting

title: Users' Expectations and Practices with Agent Memory
summary: Interviews with people who use AI tools with memory, plus analysis of online discussion posts about their experiences. Users categorise agent memories along a hierarchy from generalized knowledge to specific knowledge about the user or task, and want memories cleanly organized by those categories with access controlled accordingly.

Users desire memory organisation and access control aligned to those task-based categories
