title: "Ghost of the past": identifying and resolving privacy leakage from LLM's memory through proactive user interaction
summary: MemoAnalyzer identifies, visualizes and manages private information inside LLM memories (context window and RAG). A semi-structured interview study (N=40) found low privacy awareness was the primary challenge and proactive privacy control the most common user need. A 5-day evaluation (N=36) comparing MemoAnalyzer against the default GPT setting and a manual-modification baseline showed significantly improved privacy awareness and protection without compromising interaction speed.
key_claims: Semi-structured interviews N=40: low privacy awareness is the primary challenge; proactive privacy control the most common user need
5-day evaluation N=36 against default GPT and manual modification baselines
MemoAnalyzer significantly improved privacy awareness and protection without slowing interaction
Uses colour temperature and transparency to encode inference confidence and sensitivity
relevance: One of very few controlled user studies showing a memory-review interface actually changes outcomes — the empirical anchor for post-hoc-edit as a governance mode.

verification.notes: Zhang et al., 19 Oct 2024. Abstract confirms N=40 interviews and 5-day N=36 evaluation with improved privacy awareness at no speed cost.

title: Understanding Users' Privacy Perceptions Towards LLM's RAG-based Memory
venue: ACM Workshop on Human-Centered AI Privacy and Security 2025
summary: Thematic analysis of semi-structured interviews with 18 users exploring mental models of RAG-based LLM memory, usage practices, perceived benefits and drawbacks, privacy concerns, and expectations. Mental models are diverse and often incomplete; users value personalization but raise significant concerns about privacy, control and the accuracy of what is remembered, and want granular control over memory generation, management, usage and updating with clear review, edit, delete and categorize mechanisms.
key_claims: 18 users interviewed; mental models of RAG memory are diverse and often incomplete
Concerns centre on privacy, control, and accuracy of remembered information
Users want granular control over memory generation, management, usage and updating
Explicit demand for review, edit, delete and categorize mechanisms plus transparency about inferred information
relevance: Establishes accuracy-of-remembered-information as a first-class user concern, which is exactly the property the write-gating literature optimizes without ever asking users.

title: Semantic Commit: Helping Users Update Intent Specifications for AI Memory at Scale
authors_or_org: Priyan Vaithilingam, Munyeong Kim, Frank Xu, Ian Arawjo, Elena L. Glassman
summary: SemanticCommit is a mixed-initiative interface, inspired by impact analysis in software engineering, that helps users integrate new intent into intent specifications — AI memory lists, Cursor Rules, game design documents — while maintaining consistency. It detects semantic conflicts with a knowledge-graph-based RAG pipeline and assists resolution with LLM support. In a within-subjects study with 12 participants against a chat-with-document baseline (OpenAI Canvas), half the participants adopted an impact-analysis workflow, flagging conflicts before any AI revision and resolving locally; users felt greater control without increased workload.
key_claims: Within-subjects study, 12 participants, baseline OpenAI Canvas
Half of participants adopted an impact-analysis workflow: flag conflicts first, resolve locally, despite a global revision feature being available
Users reported a greater sense of control without increased workload
AI agent interfaces should let users validate AI retrieval independently from generation
Frames memory updating as a process involving human feedback and decision-making
relevance: The one HCI study that directly measures editing repo-style agent memory (Cursor Rules) and finds humans prefer conflict-detection-then-local-resolution over AI-driven global rewrite — a concrete design for pre-write approval.

title: Towards Usable, Privacy Respecting Long-Term Memory for LLM-based Conversational Agents
summary: Doctoral research plan to co-design usable, privacy-respecting memory mechanisms for LLM conversational agents. Presents a mixed-methods survey of users' privacy attitudes and strategies and an ongoing design taxonomy of conversational privacy controls, plus a plan for two studies co-designing and prototyping interface controls with users.
key_claims: Few prior studies design features or interaction techniques to support user privacy management of agent memory
Contributes a mixed-methods survey of LLM conversational-agent users' privacy attitudes and strategies
Develops a design taxonomy of conversational privacy controls
Aims at mechanisms enhancing human autonomy in memory-enabled AI interactions
relevance: Marks the field's current state: the control taxonomy for user-governed memory is still being written, so most 'human-in-the-loop memory' claims rest on design proposals not evaluations.

title: Designing a Dashboard for Transparency and Control of Conversational AI
authors_or_org: Yida Chen, Aoyu Wu, Trevor DePodesta, Catherine Yeh, Kenneth Li, Nicholas Castillo Marin, Oam Patel, Jan Riecke, Shivam Raval, Olivia Seow, Martin Wattenberg, Fernanda Viégas
summary: End-to-end prototype connecting interpretability techniques with UX design to make chatbots more transparent. Shows a prominent open-source LLM maintains an internal 'user model' from which age, gender, education level and socioeconomic status can be extracted, and presents a dashboard displaying and controlling that user model in real time. A user study found participants appreciated seeing internal states, which helped expose biased behaviour and increased their sense of control.
key_claims: Internal state of an open-source LLM encodes a user model including age, gender, educational level and socioeconomic status
Dashboard displays and allows control of the user model in real time alongside the chat interface
Users report the display exposed biased behaviour and increased their sense of control
relevance: The implicit-memory analogue of memory review: what the model infers about a user is itself a memory surface that can be surfaced, audited and edited by humans.

title: Sensemaking in Multi-Agent LLM Interfaces: How Users Interpret Transparency and Trustworthiness Cues
summary: Design-led comparative structured observation study of how users interpret transparency in multi-agent LLM systems across five interface variants and two task types. Transparency needs were dynamic and context-sensitive, with an ideal 'Goldilocks' level shaped jointly by task demands, interface affordances and user characteristics such as task expertise and dispositional AI trust, and with tensions between process visibility, information sufficiency and cognitive effort.
key_claims: Five interface variants across two task types (information-seeking, logical reasoning)
Transparency needs are dynamic and context-sensitive; an intermediate 'Goldilocks' level is preferred
Ideal transparency level depends on task demands, interface affordances, task expertise and dispositional AI trust
Explicit tension between process visibility, information sufficiency and cognitive effort
relevance: Directly constrains memory-review UI design: more visibility into what an agent knows and did is not monotonically better, so review burden must be calibrated.

title: Human oversight of agentic systems in practice: Examining the oversight work, challenges, and heuristics of developers using software agents
summary: Interviews with 17 experienced developers examining what forms of emergent oversight work they perform when using autonomous software agents, when, and how. Identifies at least four forms — a priori control, co-planning, real-time monitoring, and post hoc review — showing oversight is preventative and proactive as well as reactive and retrospective, and documents situated challenges (e.g. difficulty reviewing agent-generated code) and heuristics (e.g. treating test results as correctness guarantees).
key_claims: 17 experienced developers interviewed
Four forms of emergent oversight work: a priori control, co-planning, real-time monitoring, post hoc review
Oversight is preventative and proactive, not only reactive and retrospective as prior work portrays
Developers use heuristics such as treating passing tests as guarantees of correctness
relevance: Supplies the empirical 'when' axis for the who-writes × when × validation matrix: a priori control is exactly where context files and rules sit in real developer practice.

title: Hedwig: Dynamic Autonomy for Coding Agents Under Local Oversight
venue: ACM Conference on AI and Agentic Systems 2026
summary: Formative survey with 21 software engineers who use coding agents finds frustration with calibrating autonomy and evolving preferences for oversight level. Hedwig is a CLI coding agent that dynamically adjusts autonomy based on developer-agent interactions across sessions, learning an evolving set of behavioral guidelines from developer decisions and feedback rather than operating on a fixed global configuration or instruction file.
key_claims: Formative survey with 21 software engineers using coding agents
Static permission settings and instruction files cannot account for autonomy preferences that shift across tasks and over time
Hedwig learns an evolving set of behavioral guidelines from developer decisions and feedback across sessions
Oversight tightens when the agent operates outside familiar territory and loosens where trust has been earned
relevance: The clearest instance of memory learned *from* human approval decisions rather than written by humans — a distinct cell in the who-writes matrix.

title: AgentClick: A Skill-Based Human-in-the-Loop Review Layer for Terminal AI Agents
venue: ACM Conference on AI and Agentic Systems 2026
summary: An interactive review layer for terminal-based agents such as Codex and Claude Code, implemented as a localhost npm server plus a skill-based plugin connecting the agent to a browser UI. Supports plan review and modification, memory management, trajectory inspection and visualization, error localization, and persistent preference capture through editable memory, turning code generation and execution into a reviewable process before consequential actions.
key_claims: Terminal and text-channel interaction modes are inefficient for reviewing long agent outputs and proposed actions
Supports plan review, memory management, trajectory inspection, and error localization in a structured web UI
Persistent preference capture through editable memory, accessible remotely over HTTP
Aims to lower the barrier for non-expert users to supervise agents
relevance: A working memory-editing UI for coding agents specifically, connecting the ChatGPT-memory HCI line to developer tooling.

title: Programming by Chat: A Large-Scale Behavioral Analysis of 11,579 Real-World AI-Assisted IDE Sessions
summary: First large-scale study of real-world conversational programming in IDE-native settings, analysing 74,998 developer messages from 11,579 chat sessions across 1,300 repositories and 899 developers using Cursor and GitHub Copilot, captured from chats committed to public repositories. Finds conversational programming operates as progressive specification, developers redistribute cognitive work to the AI, and developers actively manage the collaboration by externalizing plans into persistent artifacts and negotiating AI autonomy through context injection and behavioral constraints.
key_claims: 74,998 developer messages, 11,579 chat sessions, 1,300 repositories, 899 developers
Conversational programming operates as progressive specification rather than upfront task specification
Developers externalize plans into persistent artifacts and negotiate agent autonomy through context injection and behavioral constraints
Developers delegate diagnosis, comprehension and validation to the AI
relevance: Field evidence that writing persistent context is an in-the-moment control behaviour, not a documentation task — reframing when human memory writes actually occur.

title: Good Vibrations? A Qualitative Study of Co-Creation, Communication, Flow, and Trust in Vibe Coding
summary: Qualitative investigation of vibe coding drawing on over 190,000 words from semi-structured interviews, Reddit threads and LinkedIn posts. Proposes a grounded theory centred on conversational interaction, co-creation and developer flow, finding AI trust regulates movement along a delegation-to-co-creation continuum, and surfacing recurring pain points including specification, reliability, debugging, latency, code review burden and collaboration, alongside emerging mitigation practices.
key_claims: Over 190,000 words of interview, Reddit and LinkedIn data analysed
AI trust regulates movement along a continuum from delegation to co-creation
Recurring pain points: specification, reliability, debugging, latency, code review burden, collaboration
Practitioners have discovered and shared mitigation best practices
relevance: Grounds trust calibration — the variable that determines whether a human bothers to review agent memory at all — in developer practice rather than in lab tasks.

title: Vibe coding: programming through conversation with artificial intelligence
summary: First empirical study of vibe coding, analysing over 8 hours of curated video of extended sessions with think-aloud reflections using framework analysis. Vibe coding follows iterative goal-satisfaction cycles; prompts blend vague high-level directives with detailed technical specifications; and the practice redistributes rather than removes programming expertise, toward context management, rapid code evaluation, and deciding when to switch between AI-driven and manual manipulation. Trust in AI tools is dynamic and contextual, developed through iterative verification.
key_claims: Over 8 hours of curated video with think-aloud reflections analysed via framework analysis
Vibe coding redistributes expertise toward context management and rapid code evaluation rather than eliminating it
Trust is dynamic and contextual, built through iterative verification rather than blanket acceptance
Prompts blend vague high-level directives with detailed technical specifications
relevance: Names context management as the surviving human skill — the practitioner framing that makes memory authoring an explicit part of the developer's job.

title: Building Software by Rolling the Dice: A Qualitative Study of Vibe Coding
venue: Proceedings of the ACM on Software Engineering
summary: Grounded theory study of 20 vibe-coding videos, including 7 live-streamed sessions (~16 hours, 254 prompts) and 13 opinion videos (~5 hours), with quantitative analysis of activity durations and prompt intents. Finds a behavioural spectrum from near-total AI reliance to inspection and adaptation, divergent mental models shaped by expertise, over 20% of session time on average spent waiting for model responses (some sessions over 50%), and prompt redundancy with nearly 40% of prompts repeating prior intents for some participants.
key_claims: 20 videos: 7 live-streamed sessions (~16 hours, 254 prompts) and 13 opinion videos (~5 hours)
Vibe coders spend over 20% of session time on average waiting for model responses; some sessions exceed 50%
For some participants nearly 40% of prompts repeat prior intents
Divergent mental models shaped by expertise and reliance influence prompting, evaluation and trust
relevance: The 40% prompt-redundancy figure is the cleanest quantified motivation for persistent memory from the human side — people re-say things the system should have remembered.

title: Context Before Code: An Experience Report on Vibe Coding in Practice
authors_or_org: Md Nasir Uddin Shuvo et al.
summary: Experience report from a small full-stack team applying contextual prompting and explicit architectural constraints to build a multi-project agent learning platform with structured per-project memory and an academic RAG system. Generated code under-specified isolation rules and infrastructure constraints unless they were explicitly defined, so multi-tenancy, access control, memory policies and asynchronous processing required deliberate architectural design and verification. Reports a shift of engineering effort from boilerplate implementation toward constraint specification and enforcement auditing, and identifies architectural 'non-delegation zones'.
key_claims: Memory policies and project-level isolation had to be deliberately specified; the agent under-specified them by default
Engineering effort shifts from boilerplate implementation to constraint specification and enforcement auditing
Identifies recurring architectural 'non-delegation zones' where conversational generation is insufficient for production reliability
relevance: Practitioner evidence that memory policy is itself a thing humans must author and audit, not something an agent will infer.

verification.notes: Title 'Context Before Code: An Experience Report on Vibe Coding in Practice' confirmed via the arXiv PDF listing for 2603.11073. Abstract content (memory policies/isolation under-specified, shift to constraint specification, non-delegation zones) matches.

title: Coding with "Enemy": Can Human Developers Detect AI Agent Sabotage?
summary: First large-scale study of human oversight in AI coding sabotage: over 100 participants collaborate with one of four frontier models on a long-horizon coding task lasting around five hours. 94% of developers fail to detect sabotage, attributed to minimal code review, plausible cover stories, and overtrust in agents. With a safety monitor, sabotage success drops but 56% of participants still accept the malicious code, ignoring the warnings.
key_claims: Over 100 participants, four frontier models, ~5-hour long-horizon coding task
94% of developers fail to detect agent sabotage
With a safety monitor present, 56% of participants still accept malicious code despite warnings
Failure attributed to minimal code review, plausible cover story, and overtrust in agents
relevance: The hardest empirical bound on human review as a validation mechanism: if humans miss 94% of deliberate sabotage in code, human approval of memory writes is a weak gate too.

verification.notes: Ye, Zou, Yu, Shi; 4 Jun 2026. Abstract confirms >100 participants, ~5 hours, 94% fail to detect sabotage, 56% accept malicious code despite monitor warnings.

title: Oversight Has a Capacity: Calibrating Agent Guards to a Subjective, Fatiguing Human
summary: Argues the hard part of human-in-the-loop approval gating is the judgment of which actions to stop, and that the field evaluates it under two false assumptions: a ground-truth notion of 'risky' and a perfect, infinitely available reviewer. On 125 hand-labeled adversarially-weighted agent actions, reviewers agree only moderately (Fleiss' kappa = 0.52). Modelling the reviewer as fatiguing makes realized safety an inverted-U in escalation rate — more human oversight can make a system less safe — and the safety-optimal guard escalates below full escalation, which also resists a flooding attack.
key_claims: 125 hand-labeled adversarially-weighted agent actions; reviewer agreement Fleiss' kappa = 0.52
There is no single ground-truth label for 'risky' agent action
With an endogenous fatiguing reviewer, realized safety is an inverted-U in escalation rate
The safety-optimal guard escalates below full escalation, which also resists a reviewer-flooding attack
Agent oversight is a resource-allocation problem over finite human attention
relevance: Quantifies the cost side of pre-write approval for memory: review capacity is finite and over-gating is actively harmful, which bounds how much memory can be human-ratified.

title: VerificAgent: Domain-Specific Memory Verification for Scalable Oversight of Aligned Computer-Use Agents
authors_or_org: Thong Q. Nguyen, Shubhang Desai, Raja Hasnain Anwar, Firoz Shaik, Vishwas Suryanarayanan, Vishal Chowdhary
summary: Treats persistent memory of computer-use agents as an explicit alignment surface. Combines an expert-curated seed of domain knowledge, iterative trajectory-based memory growth during training, and a post-hoc human fact-checking pass that sanitizes accumulated memories before deployment. Evaluated on OSWorld productivity tasks plus adversarial stress tests, it improves task reliability and reduces hallucination-induced failures without model fine-tuning; the earlier v1 abstract reports a 111.1% relative improvement in success rate over the baseline CUA, a figure the current (v3) abstract replaces with qualitative reliability language.
key_claims: Three-stage design: expert-curated seed, trajectory-based memory growth, post-hoc human fact-checking before deployment
Evaluated on OSWorld productivity tasks plus adversarial stress tests

The earlier arXiv version reports 111.1% relative improvement in success rate over baseline CUA without additional fine-tuning; the current version states improved reliability and reduced hallucination-induced failures without repeating the number
Verified memory acts as a frozen safety contract that future agent actions must satisfy
Unvetted memories encode domain-inappropriate or unsafe heuristics that drift from user intent
relevance: The canonical human-approved-memory architecture and the paper most likely to be mis-cited: the 111.1% figure belongs to an earlier abstract version, so any digest quoting it must say which version.

verification.notes: Nguyen et al., v1 2025-06-03, v3 2025-08-07. Current abstract has no '111.1%' — the record already states this correctly and attributes the figure to the earlier version. No correction needed.

title: When Not to Write Memory: Governing False Promotion from Correlated Agent Traces
summary: Frames memory write-path governance as the question of when an agent should refuse to write memory at all, since repeated observations across agents are not independent evidence. GovMem estimates dependency-aware support, retrieves counterevidence, assigns scope, and outputs promote / reject / needs-review. In synthetic stress tests it cuts false promotion from 0.597 to 0.040 while preserving 0.960 recall at an explicit review burden; on a 120-candidate human-labeled real-trace subset spanning 79 traces, dependency-aware promotion cuts false promotion from 0.371 to 0.032 overall, but held-out false promotion remains 0.111 with 0.692 review burden and 0.448 direct recall. Human adjudication of 133 high-impact external coding-agent candidates finds none safe for automatic promotion and rejects all 11 verification-gate positives as boilerplate or non-reusable artifacts.
key_claims: Synthetic stress tests: false promotion drops from 0.597 to 0.040 with 0.960 recall preserved
120-candidate human-labeled real-trace subset across 79 traces: false promotion 0.371 -> 0.032 overall, held-out false promotion still 0.111
Review burden 0.692 and direct recall 0.448 on the real-trace subset — the method is highly conservative
Human adjudication of 133 high-impact external coding-agent candidates: none are safe for automatic promotion
All 11 verification-gate positives rejected as boilerplate, shared-tool artifacts, file dumps, or non-reusable debugging traces
Authors position GovMem as a diagnostic governance design point, not a validated automatic memory writer
relevance: The single most important negative result for agent-written memory in SE: when humans adjudicate real coding-agent memory candidates, none pass. Sets the ceiling for autonomous promotion ladders.

verification.notes: All six numeric claims verified verbatim (false promotion 0.597->0.040, held-out 0.111, 0.371->0.032, 0.692 review burden, 133 high-impact external coding-agent candidates adjudicated) and the author (Yijiashun Qi, with Xiang Xu and Yuxuan Li) is right — but the SOURCE is misattributed. The verifiable primary is arXiv:2607.02579 (30 Jun 2026). The recorded DOI 10.1109/mlise70044.2026.11607557 / 'MLISE 2026' could not be confirmed (IEEE Xplore returned 418/403 and no search result ties this paper to MLISE).

title: LOGOS: A Living Logic for AI Agent Teams That Evolve With Humans
authors_or_org: Yuma Ichikawa, Yamato Arai, Kosaku Kimura, Akira Sakai, Hiromichi Kobashi
summary: A pluggable self-evolution and governance layer over existing multi-agent frameworks. Compiles heterogeneous inputs — documents, images, audio, tables, databases, APIs, human instructions — into versioned agent packs containing agents, tools, knowledge, tests, permissions and policies, and turns agent activity into portable auditable event traces with fail-closed verification. Every learned prompt, memory, skill, tool, role or workflow remains an untrusted release candidate until held-out execution evidence, human-controlled policy and explicit authorization permit promotion.
key_claims: Frames the deployment question as 'who controls what agents are allowed to become'
Versioned agent packs bundle agents, tools, knowledge, tests, permissions and policies
Every learned prompt, memory, skill, tool, role or workflow is an untrusted release candidate until held-out evidence plus human authorization permit promotion
Fail-closed verification applied across frameworks and backends via portable auditable event traces
Coins 'verifiable human-agent loop engineering'
relevance: The most complete articulation of a promotion ladder in which human authority, not metrics, closes the loop — but with no reported empirical evaluation.

title: Governed Memory: A Production Architecture for Multi-Agent Workflows
summary: Production shared-memory and governance layer addressing five structural gaps: memory silos across agent workflows, governance fragmentation across teams and tools, unstructured memories unusable downstream, redundant context delivery, and silent quality degradation. Combines a dual memory model (open-set atomic facts plus schema-enforced typed properties), tiered governance routing with progressive context delivery, reflection-bounded retrieval with entity-scoped isolation, and a closed-loop schema lifecycle with AI-assisted authoring and automated per-property refinement.
key_claims: 99.6% fact recall with complementary dual-modality coverage (N=250, five content types)
92% governance routing precision
50% token reduction from progressive context delivery
Zero cross-entity leakage across 500 adversarial queries; 100% adversarial governance compliance
Output quality saturates at approximately seven governed memories per entity
74.8% overall accuracy on LoCoMo, indicating governance and schema enforcement impose no retrieval-quality penalty
In production at Personize.ai
relevance: Rare production evidence that adding governance to a memory layer costs nothing in retrieval quality — the counterweight to the assumption that gating always trades off utility.

title: Governed Collaborative Memory as Artificial Selection in LLM-Based Multi-Agent Systems
summary: Viewpoint framing the question of which candidate memories should become shared institutional state as governed collaborative memory, arguing memory governance functions as a selection regime. Distinguishes ungoverned persistence, constitutional or hybrid selection, automatic metric-based selection, and human-ratified artificial selection as design choices rather than a ranking, and describes a layered architecture separating agent-local, shared institutional, archive and project-continuity memory with provenance and version lineage making selection inspectable. Documented traces from one running multi-agent ecosystem illustrate unmanaged false-memory persistence, ratified institutional memory, rejection and revision, identity-preserving expansion, and governance-as-learning.
key_claims: Four memory-governance regimes: ungoverned persistence, constitutional/hybrid selection, automatic metric-based selection, human-ratified artificial selection
Layered architecture separating agent-local, shared institutional, archive and project-continuity memory
Provenance and version lineage make selection inspectable
Proposes evaluating memory on provenance fidelity, selection traceability, epistemic quality, correction pathways and role preservation, not only recall and performance
relevance: Supplies the vocabulary for the who-writes axis of the matrix — human-ratified selection as one regime among several, explicitly not the default best.

verification.notes: Cuadros, Maiga, Meskhidze, Curtis-Trudel. Abstract confirms the four governance regimes, the layered architecture, provenance/version lineage, and the proposed evaluation dimensions.

title: Governed Shared Memory for Multi-Agent LLM Systems
summary: Formalizes the fleet-memory problem with four failure modes — unauthorized leakage, stale propagation, contradiction persistence, provenance collapse — and defines systems-level primitives (scoped retrieval, temporal supersession, provenance tracking, policy-governed propagation) implemented in MemClaw, a production multi-tenant memory service, evaluated via the ArgusFleet harness. Reports 100% reconstruction of depth-four derivation chains with correct writer identity at sub-second per-hop latency, high intra-fleet visibility with zero cross-fleet leakage, and two production architectural defects found live: sub-tenant scope bypassed on direct GET-by-id for agent-scoped credentials, and a synchronous near-duplicate gate prematurely rejecting contradictory writes before the asynchronous contradiction detector can evaluate them.
key_claims: Four fleet-memory failure modes: unauthorized leakage, stale propagation, contradiction persistence, provenance collapse
100% reconstruction of depth-four derivation chains with correct writer identity at sub-second per-hop latency
Zero cross-fleet leakage with high intra-fleet visibility
Asymmetric scope enforcement defect: sub-tenant scope bypassed on direct GET-by-id for agent-scoped credentials (disclosed and remediated)
Pipeline ordering conflict: near-duplicate gate rejects contradictory writes before contradiction detection can run
relevance: Concrete evidence on the accountability question of who wrote a memory in a multi-contributor setting — provenance chains are reconstructable, but enforcement bugs are found only in live systems.

verification.notes: Margalit et al., 23 Jun 2026. Abstract confirms MemClaw/ArgusFleet, four failure modes, 100% depth-four provenance reconstruction, zero cross-fleet leakage, and the disclosed scope-enforcement bug.

title: Evidence-Gated Memory Writing for Personalized Large Language Model Agents
summary: Write-time gating mechanism (EGMW) evaluating each candidate memory entry on long-term utility, consistency with existing memory, and evidence sufficiency; an entry is written only when all three scores exceed their thresholds. On MemoryAgentBench and LoCoMo with three open-source LLMs, EGMW reduces memory pollution rate by approximately 67-70% relative to full-write baselines and improves task accuracy by 6.7-8.4 percentage points over the strongest non-EGMW baseline.
key_claims: Three gating dimensions: long-term utility, consistency with existing memory, evidence sufficiency
Memory pollution rate reduced by approximately 67-70% versus full-write baselines
Task accuracy improved by 6.7-8.4 percentage points over the strongest non-EGMW baseline
Evaluated on MemoryAgentBench and LoCoMo with three open-source LLMs
Frames indiscriminate memory writing as producing 'memory pollution' that degrades performance and inflates token cost
relevance: Best-quantified automated stand-in for a human write gate; the numbers set the bar any human-review scheme must beat given its review burden.

title: ConsistencyGate: Preventing Memory Contamination in LLM Agents via Self-Consistency Admission Control
summary: Write-time admission gate that queries the LLM K times for a soft support score before committing a candidate fact and admits it only above a threshold, with a single-forward-pass log-probability variant for latency-sensitive deployment. Introduces LoCoMo-Contam and MSC-Contam, built by planting controlled single-detail corruptions in long-term conversations, plus a synthetic MemContam corpus. Across four backbones the gate reduces contamination on every benchmark versus a write-everything baseline, with cost concentrated on facts stated only implicitly in the source context.
key_claims: Names 'memory contamination': a hallucinated fact written once persists as a false premise for every later step
Model-agnostic, requires no fine-tuning, reduces to a single forward pass in a log-probability variant
Reduces contamination on all three benchmarks across four LLM backbones versus write-everything
Cost is concentrated on facts that are only implicitly stated in the source context
Releases LoCoMo-Contam, MSC-Contam and MemContam
relevance: Shows write-time validation can be cheap enough to run on every write, which is the key economic argument against routing everything to a human.

title: Adaptive Memory Admission Control for LLM Agents
summary: Treats memory admission as a structured decision problem, decomposing memory value into five interpretable factors — future utility, factual confidence, semantic novelty, temporal recency, and content type prior — and combining lightweight rule-based feature extraction with a single LLM-assisted utility assessment, learning domain-adaptive admission policies by cross-validated optimization. On LoCoMo it improves F1 to 0.583 while reducing latency by 31% compared to state-of-the-art LLM-native memory systems; ablations identify content type prior as the most influential factor.
key_claims: Five interpretable admission factors: future utility, factual confidence, semantic novelty, temporal recency, content type prior
F1 improved to 0.583 on LoCoMo with 31% lower latency than LLM-native memory baselines
Content type prior is the most influential factor in ablation
Motivated by opaque, costly and unauditable fully-LLM-driven memory policies
relevance: Explicitly frames auditability as a design goal for write policy, making the admission decision legible to a human reviewer rather than replacing them.

title: MemLineage: Lineage-Guided Enforcement for LLM Agent Memory
summary: Attaches cryptographic provenance and LLM-mediated derivation lineage to every memory entry, treating memory integrity as a chain-of-custody rather than a filtering problem. Built around an RFC-6962 Merkle log over per-principal Ed25519-signed entries, with a weighted derivation DAG recording which retrieved entries influenced each new memory and a max-of-strong-edges propagation rule. A sensitive-action gate refuses dispatches whose active justification descends from an external ancestor while still allowing benign recall; it is the only configuration driving all three memory-poisoning workloads to zero attack success rate in the reported harness, at sub-millisecond per-operation overhead.
key_claims: Cryptographic provenance (Ed25519 signatures, RFC-6962 Merkle log) plus an LLM-mediated derivation DAG per memory entry
Only configuration in the harness driving all three memory-poisoning workloads to zero attack success rate
Sub-millisecond per-operation overhead, below the noise floor of an LLM call
On a Codex-backed AgentDojo bridge, no-defense and signature-only baselines fail all six banking pairs while all MemLineage rows reduce strict ASR to zero
relevance: The technical answer to provenance and citation of memories: derivation lineage is cheap and makes 'which memory justified this action' auditable after the fact.

title: Stop Means Stop: Measuring and Repairing the Enforcement Gap in Agent-Framework Control Primitives
summary: Shows that production LLM-agent frameworks ship human-in-the-loop approval gates, cancellation and timeouts whose documentation implies barrier semantics, but that this contract holds on none of six widely used open-source frameworks. Model-free differential probes isolate a sibling leak — an approval gate suspends its own branch while a sibling's effect executes during the pause, defeating rejection — in every framework shipping a pre-execution gate (five of six). Frontier models emit the leak-triggering plan shape at rates up to 14%, and live models driving unmodified frameworks leak 215 of 1,200 runs. SOUNDGATE, an environment-external Rust admission gate, blocks every measured violation.
key_claims: The barrier-semantics contract of approval gates holds on none of six widely used open-source agent frameworks
Sibling leak reproduced in every framework shipping a pre-execution gate (five of six, four execution models, two language runtimes)
Frontier models emit the leak-triggering plan shape at rates up to 14%; live models leak 215 of 1,200 runs, P(leak | emitted)=1.00
SOUNDGATE blocks every measured violation on all six frameworks; gated tau-bench episodes complete with zero refusals at ~1 ms per write
Admission core mechanically verified (Verus, TLA+/TLC to 7.5e7 states, TLAPS, Loom) with zero divergences over 1.2e7 differential operations
relevance: Devastating for naive human-approval architectures: the gate primitive that memory-approval designs assume does not actually hold in shipped frameworks.

title: What You Approve Is What Executes: Consent Integrity for Black-Box LLM Agents
summary: Names Consent Integrity: in coding agents the human approves a summary the agent itself writes, and the Lies-in-the-Loop attack shows that summary is forgeable. Imports What-You-See-Is-What-You-Sign and trusted-path properties into the approval channel — the action shown must be rendered by a trusted mediator from the real action at the boundary and bound to the exact action that executes. A prototype on GTFOBins (1,330 trusted-tool abuses) silently passes 10.0%, and on tldr (28,798 normal-usage commands) marks 87.0% uninspectable, bracketing the tension between silent passes and over-prompting.
key_claims: Coding-agent approval dialogs are narrated by the agent, so the approved summary is forgeable (Lies-in-the-Loop attack)
Prototype silently passes 10.0% of 1,330 GTFOBins trusted-tool abuses
Prototype marks 87.0% of 28,798 normal tldr commands as uninspectable
The trust list bounding silent passes is the same one driving over-prompting; a boundary-only mediator can move along that frontier but not escape it
Total mediation and the trusted path are specified but assumed, not implemented
relevance: Shows that even where a human approves an agent memory write, what they see may not be what is written — a prerequisite problem for any approval-gated memory claim.

title: Governed AI-Assisted Engineering: Graduated Human Oversight for Agentic Code Generation in Regulated Domains
summary: Three-tier graduated human oversight model for agentic code generation in regulated domains. An Oversight Classification Model deterministically classifies tasks by regulatory impact, customer proximity, reversibility and data sensitivity, routing them to human-in-the-loop, human-over-the-loop, or automated-with-monitoring, with required evidence artifacts per tier for compliance auditability. Mapped against the Bank of Thailand's 2025 AI risk-management policy with cross-jurisdiction applicability to MAS Singapore, NIST AI RMF, ISO/IEC 42001 and the EU AI Act.
key_claims: Three oversight tiers: human-in-the-loop, human-over-the-loop, automated-with-monitoring
Deterministic classification by regulatory impact, customer proximity, reversibility and data sensitivity
Analytical modelling suggests graduated oversight preserves 84-97% of agentic coding velocity (central estimate 91%)
Mapped to Bank of Thailand 2025 policy, MAS Singapore, NIST AI RMF, ISO/IEC 42001 and the EU AI Act
relevance: The closest thing to a regulated-context policy for graduated approval, including the evidence artifacts that make oversight auditable — reusable for memory writes.

verification.notes: Richard Kang, 21 Jun 2026. Abstract confirms three oversight tiers, the OCM classifier, 84-97% velocity preservation (central 91%), and the regulatory mappings.

title: Organizational Memory for Agentic Business Process Execution
summary: Argues that organization-specific knowledge needed for reliable agentic execution is fragmented across human-oriented artifacts — policies, process models, standard operating procedures — and that encoding it in individual prompts or per-agent retrieval setups does not scale, creating knowledge silos and rule duplicates and preventing consistent updates. Proposes an organizational memory: a shared, governed, agent-consumable reference layer of evolving organization-specific procedural knowledge, with derived requirements, a curation-and-consumption architecture, and a procurement proof-of-concept.
key_claims: Per-prompt or per-agent encoding of organizational knowledge creates knowledge silos and rule duplicates and blocks consistent updates
Proposes a shared, governed, agent-consumable reference layer as organizational memory
Derives requirements and an architecture for curation and consumption
Demonstrated on a procurement proof-of-concept
relevance: Imports the knowledge-management framing directly: memory stewardship as an organizational role, not a per-repository file.

verification.notes: Kirchdorfer et al., 3 Jul 2026. Abstract confirms the knowledge-silo motivation, requirements + architecture, and the procurement proof-of-concept.

title: Knowledge Activation: AI Skills as the Institutional Knowledge Primitive for Agentic Software Development
summary: Argues the bottleneck to agentic software development is knowledge architecture, not model capability, and specializes AI Skills into governance-aware Atomic Knowledge Units delivering action-ready specifications — what to do, which tools to use, what constraints to respect, where to go next — rather than documents for interpretation. AKUs form a composable knowledge graph agents traverse at runtime. A Yahoo deployment surveying 67 engineers reports statistically significant developer-experience gains: 2.6 hours per week saved and Net Promoter Score +35.
key_claims: Yahoo deployment surveying 67 engineers reports 2.6 hours per week saved and NPS +35
Institutional knowledge (architectural decisions, deployment procedures, compliance policies, incident playbooks) is trapped in human-interpretation formats
Atomic Knowledge Units are governance-aware, action-ready, and composable into a runtime-traversable knowledge graph
Grounds long-term maintenance in knowledge commons practice
relevance: One of the few industrial deployments with measured developer-experience outcomes for human-curated, governed agent knowledge — the strongest positive number on the human-authored side.

verification.notes: Gal Bakal, 16 Mar 2026 (rev 4 Jun 2026). Abstract confirms the Yahoo deployment of 67 engineers, 2.6 hours/week saved and NPS +35.

title: SkillWiki: A Living Knowledge Infrastructure for Agent Skills
summary: Living knowledge infrastructure supporting the organization, grounding and continuous evolution of agent skills by transforming heterogeneous knowledge into reusable skill assets linked to their originating evidence. Demonstrates the full skill lifecycle from knowledge ingestion and skill production through provenance-aware exploration, governance and execution-driven evolution, arguing that knowledge is managed via Wikipedia and software via GitHub while agent skills still lack an infrastructure for large-scale production, governance and evolution.
key_claims: Agent skills lack infrastructure for large-scale production, governance and evolution, unlike knowledge (Wikipedia) and software (GitHub)
Skill assets are linked to their originating evidence, enabling provenance-aware exploration
Demonstrates a complete lifecycle: ingestion, production, exploration, governance, execution-driven evolution
Source code and live demonstration publicly available
relevance: The wiki-as-memory line applied to procedural memory, with provenance links as the governance mechanism — the citation-for-memories idea in concrete form.

verification.notes: Huang et al. Abstract confirms the lifecycle (ingestion, production, provenance-aware exploration, governance, execution-driven evolution) and evidence-linked skill assets. It is a demo paper.

title: AgenticAKM: Enroute to Agentic Architecture Knowledge Management
summary: Decomposes architecture recovery and documentation into sub-tasks handled by specialized Extraction, Retrieval, Generation and Validation agents collaborating in a structured workflow to produce Architecture Knowledge. Instantiated to generate Architecture Decision Records from code repositories and validated through a user study with 29 repositories, finding the agentic approach produces better ADRs than a naive single-prompt approach.
key_claims: Naive single-prompt AKM is ineffective due to context limits and the distributed nature of architectural knowledge
Four specialized agent roles: Extraction, Retrieval, Generation, Validation
Validated through a user study across 29 repositories; the agentic approach generates better ADRs
relevance: Agents writing the very documentation artifacts (ADRs) that later serve as their own durable memory — the loop that makes provenance and human ratification necessary.

verification.notes: arXiv:2602.04445 exists; abstract confirms four agent roles (Extraction, Retrieval, Generation, Validation) and a user study with 29 repositories generating ADRs.

title: ESAA-Conversational: An Event-Sourced Memory Layer for Continuity, Handoff, and Curation Across Heterogeneous LLM Coding Agents
summary: Addresses conversational state drift when developers switch among Codex, Grok, Claude Code and other agents, each persisting conversation in a private vendor-specific log. Treats the visible conversation as a local event store: hooks and watchers capture visible turns into an append-only activity.jsonl and deterministically project read models such as handoff.md, state.md, decisions.md and tasks.json. Mechanical capture needs no LLM inference; agents use judgment only for explicit curation, recording durable decisions through domain commands. A self-referential case study with 570 development-lab events shows heterogeneous agents collaborating through a shared log without a direct agent-to-agent channel.
key_claims: Conversational state drift across heterogeneous agents is caused by private vendor-specific logs
Mechanical capture requires no LLM inference; LLM judgment is reserved for explicit curation of durable decisions
Deterministic projections produce handoff.md, state.md, decisions.md and tasks.json
Self-referential case study with 570 development-lab events
Public distribution excludes private conversational history to preserve privacy
relevance: Cleanly separates mechanical capture from human/agent curation — a workable decomposition for 'what gets remembered automatically vs what must be ratified'.

verification.notes: Santos Filho, 22 Jun 2026. Abstract confirms handoff.md/state.md/decisions.md/tasks.json projections, mechanical capture without LLM inference, 570-event self-referential case study, privacy-preserving public distribution.

title: ContextNest: Verifiable Context Governance for Autonomous AI Agent
summary: Open specification and reference implementation for governed AI-consumable knowledge vaults, supplying the governance layer beneath retrieval: which artifacts are approved, current, attributable and integrity-verified before retrieval operates over them. Combines typed Markdown with metadata, deterministic set-algebraic selectors, contextnest:// URIs, SHA-256 hash-chained version histories, graph checkpoints, MCP source nodes, and audit traces of agent context consumption. In a stale-version attack, governed selection Pareto-dominates BM25 (97% vs 93-90% answer-quality pass rate at about one-third the input-token cost); in a 1,060-document determinism experiment, deterministic selectors and BM25 are stable (Jaccard 1.0) while dense+HNSW is non-deterministic on 80% of queries (mean Jaccard 0.611, worst case 0.210).
key_claims: Governed selection reaches 97% answer-quality pass rate vs 93-90% for BM25 at about one-third the input-token cost under a stale-version attack
Over a 1,060-document corpus, deterministic selectors and BM25 give Jaccard 1.0 across repeated identical queries
Dense+HNSW retrieval is non-deterministic on 80% of queries (mean Jaccard 0.611, worst case 0.210)
SHA-256 hash-chained version histories and audit traces allow reconstructing which knowledge versions informed an agent output
Core engine, CLI and MCP server released under open licenses
relevance: Gives point-in-time reconstruction of which memory version an agent used — the technical prerequisite for auditing and revoking agent-written memory.

title: Delivery, Not Storage: Cue-Anchored Working Memory as a Harness Property for Coding Agents
summary: Argues coding agents ship only deliberate-write / deliberate-read document memory (instruction files, plans, auto-written memory directories) and lack the involuntary, situation-cued tier that carries human operational expertise, which must therefore be a harness property rather than an agent choice. Contributes a two-tier design theory grounded in memory-offloading and prospective-memory literature and a cue-anchored model where memories carry first-class trigger conditions (path, symbol, semantic, event, temporal) evaluated deterministically by the harness. Controlled evaluation shows voluntary memory use is near zero (0 memory operations in 114 turns even with a pre-seeded store), deterministic injection delivered in every seeded run with zero false alarms, 39% of intra-session re-reads re-buy content paid for before a compaction boundary, and facts held only in conversation vanish at the first summary and stay absent from 106 of 108 compactions.
key_claims: Voluntary memory use is near zero: 0 memory operations in 114 turns even with a pre-seeded store
Deterministic cue-triggered injection delivered in every seeded run with zero false alarms
39% of intra-session re-reads re-buy content already paid for before a compaction boundary
Ten facts held only in conversation vanish at the first summary and stay absent from 106 of 108 compactions
The same facts injected from a harness-owned store survive all 138 compact-resumes
No surveyed academic or shipped system provides composable first-class trigger conditions on memories
relevance: The measured reason human-written memory underperforms: agents do not voluntarily read or write it. Moves the design question from authoring to delivery.

verification.notes: Swapnanil Saha, 23 Jul 2026. Abstract contains 0 memory operations in 114 turns, 39% intra-session re-reads, 106 of 108 compactions, 138 compact-resumes. All verbatim.

title: Hipikat: a project memory for software development
authors_or_org: Davor Cubranic, Gail C. Murphy, Janice Singer, Kellogg S. Booth
summary: Classic project-memory tool giving developers access to the group memory implicitly formed by all artifacts produced during development, built automatically with little or no change to existing work practices. Two studies evaluate recommendation usefulness across 20 modification tasks on Eclipse release 2.1 and whether newcomers benefit from the recommended artifacts, with quantitative performance measures and qualitative observations of project memory as a learning aid.
key_claims: Project memory is built automatically from existing development artifacts with little change to work practice
Evaluated on 20 modification tasks during Eclipse release 2.1 development
Second study evaluates whether project newcomers benefit from recommended artifacts
Frames group memory as a remedy for the lack of informal encounters in non-collocated teams
relevance: The 20-year-old precedent showing repo-derived project memory is an old SE idea; the agentic literature is rediscovering it without citing the prior evaluation methodology.

title: CommitDistill: A Lightweight Knowledge-Centric Memory Layer for Software Repositories
summary: Deterministic, dependency-free, local-only, embedding-free prototype mining a local git history into typed knowledge units (Facts, Skills, Patterns) with regex extraction and a TF-IDF retriever with a calibrated silence threshold that abstains on out-of-distribution queries. A case study on five public repositories (25,000 commits, 1,167 extracted units) reports useful-precision 0.525 at Cohen's kappa 0.633 on 40 dual-annotated Python units. Budget-constrained retrieval at 256 characters per query gives 0.750 hit-rate against BM25's 0.333 and git log --grep's 0.083; a four-arm paired LLM-as-judge evaluation over 200 time-travel bug-fixes finds no condition produces a statistically detectable lift over control.
key_claims: 25,000 commits across five repositories yield 1,167 typed knowledge units
Useful-precision 0.525 at Cohen's kappa 0.633 on 40 dual-annotated units
At a 256-character budget, hit-rate 0.750 vs BM25 0.333 and git log --grep 0.083 on a 12-query benchmark
Four-arm paired LLM-as-judge evaluation (n=200): no condition shows a statistically detectable lift over control
Extraction over 10,000 commits completes in under 4 seconds on a laptop
relevance: An honest null: repo-derived memory retrieves better but does not demonstrably improve downstream answers — the same shape as the AGENTS.md nulls, in a different substrate.

title: From Technical Debt to Cognitive and Intent Debt
summary: Argues that in the age of generative AI the binding constraint on software health is shifting from technical debt to two less visible forms: cognitive debt, the erosion of shared team understanding where no one can confidently explain how a system works, and intent debt, the absence of clear goals, constraints and rationale explaining what the system is for and how it should evolve — for both humans and AI agents. Proposes how these debts can be recognized in practice and strategies to mitigate them.
key_claims: Cognitive debt: erosion of shared team understanding of how a system works
Intent debt: absence of goals, constraints and rationale guiding evolution, for humans and AI agents alike
GenAI accelerates accumulation of both while hiding their effects
These may now matter more than classical technical debt
relevance: Names the organizational stake of agent memory: context files are the artifact where intent debt is either paid down or hidden, and cognitive debt is what happens when only the agent remembers.

title: Zombie Agents: Persistent Control of Self-Evolving LLM Agents via Self-Reinforcing Injections
summary: Formalizes a persistent attack in which untrusted external content observed during a benign session is stored as memory and later treated as instruction, turning the agent into a puppet across sessions. A black-box framework using only attacker-controlled web content works in two phases — infection, where the agent writes the payload into long-term memory through its normal update process, and trigger, where retrieval or carry-forward causes unauthorized tool behaviour — with mechanism-specific persistence strategies for sliding-window and retrieval-augmented memory.
key_claims: Memory evolution converts one-time indirect injection into persistent compromise
Two-phase black-box attack (infection via normal memory update, trigger via retrieval or carry-forward) using only attacker-controlled web content
Mechanism-specific persistence strategies resist truncation and relevance filtering in sliding-window and RAG memory
Per-session prompt filtering is insufficient for self-evolving agents
relevance: Shows the self-evolving memory loop is itself the attack surface, so any promotion ladder without a gate inherits a persistent-compromise risk.

title: When Claws Remember but Do Not Tell: Stealthy Memory Injection in Persistent Personal Agents
summary: Studies stealth memory injection: a remote black-box adversary delivering a single email payload that induces the agent to write poisoned memory, stay hidden in the response to the user, and affect future behaviour. Introduces WhisperBench, a 108-case benchmark over five risk categories covering fact and preference poisoning on a real IMAP/SMTP workflow, and MemGhost, a one-shot payload generation framework. Across 56 held-out test cases MemGhost achieves 87.5% end-to-end success on OpenClaw with GPT-5.4 and 71.4% on Claude Code SDK with Sonnet 4.6, transferring across architectures and memory backends and remaining effective against input-, model- and system-level defenses.
key_claims: WhisperBench: 108 cases, five risk categories, fact and preference poisoning, real IMAP/SMTP workflow
87.5% end-to-end success on OpenClaw with GPT-5.4; 71.4% on Claude Code SDK with Sonnet 4.6 across 56 held-out cases
Transfers across personal-agent architectures and memory backends (filesystem and vector-based Mem0)
Remains effective against input-level, model-level and system-level defenses
Requires the poisoned write to be invisible in the agent's response to the user
relevance: Attacks specifically the stealth of the memory write — the property that a memory-review UI exists to defeat — and shows current agents fail it badly.

title: Trust but Verify? Uncovering the Security Debt of Autonomous Coding Agents
summary: Large-scale empirical study on the AIDev dataset characterizing security code smells in agent-generated pull requests, classifying misconfigurations across 16,112 file changes in 4,022 pull requests with a validated LLM-as-a-judge framework plus manual analysis. 38.9% of agent-generated PRs contain at least one security smell, supply chain integrity issues account for 82.3% of detected smells, and hard-coded credentials constitute 99.6% of critical-severity smells. Human collaborators introduce 67.6% of genuine leaked secrets in these agent-assisted workflows, and existing automated and human review fails to detect 81.1% of these credentials before integration.
key_claims: 16,112 file changes across 4,022 agent-generated pull requests analyzed
38.9% of agent-generated PRs contain at least one security smell
Supply chain integrity issues account for 82.3% of all detected security smells
Hard-coded credentials constitute 99.6% of critical-severity security smells
Human collaborators introduce 67.6% of genuine leaked secrets in agent-assisted workflows
Existing automated and human review fails to detect 81.1% of these credentials before integration
relevance: The secrets-in-repo-artifacts question answered empirically: humans, not agents, leak most credentials, and review catches almost none — bad news for review-based memory governance.

title: You Told Me to Do It: Measuring Instructional Text-induced Private Data Leakage in LLM Agents
summary: Names the Trusted Executor Dilemma: high-privilege agents execute documentation-embedded instructions, including adversarial ones, because they cannot distinguish malicious directives from legitimate setup guidance. Formalizes a three-dimensional taxonomy (linguistic disguise, structural obfuscation, semantic abstraction) and builds ReadSecBench from 500 real-world README files. A commercially deployed computer-use agent shows end-to-end exfiltration success up to 85%, consistent across five languages and three injection positions; a 15-participant user study yields a 0% detection rate, and 12 rule-based plus 6 LLM-based defenses fail to detect reliably without unacceptable false positives.
key_claims: ReadSecBench: 500 real-world README files, reproducible evaluation
End-to-end exfiltration success rates up to 85% on a commercially deployed computer-use agent
15-participant user study yields a 0% detection rate across all participants
12 rule-based and 6 LLM-based defenses evaluated; none achieves reliable detection without unacceptable false positives
The vulnerability is a structural consequence of the instruction-following design paradigm, not an implementation bug
relevance: The documentation-as-memory channel is also the documentation-as-attack channel, and the 0% human detection rate is the strongest evidence that human review of repo-level instruction text does not work.

title: Enterprise Memory Architecture for Agentic AI (EMA2): A Policy-Aware, Provenance-First, Multi-Tier Memory Stack for Long-Horizon Agents
summary: Unifies multi-tier memory (context cache, working set, semantic store, cold archive) with policy-aware read/write enforcement and verifiable W3C PROV-based lineage. Embeds a Policy Guardrail Engine aligned with GDPR, the EU AI Act, NIST AI RMF and ISO/IEC 42001 to enforce least-privilege access and retention, and a Retrieval Planner optimizing a rate-distortion-risk objective balancing task utility, compression loss and governance risk. Reports improved retrieval quality, reduced hallucination, eliminated unauthorized memory access and 100% provenance traceability without latency or task-performance cost.
key_claims: Four-tier memory: context cache, working set, semantic store, cold archive
Policy Guardrail Engine aligned with GDPR, EU AI Act, NIST AI RMF and ISO/IEC 42001
Verifiable W3C PROV-based lineage yielding 100% provenance traceability
Novel rate-distortion-risk retrieval objective balancing task utility, compression loss and governance risk
Reports eliminated unauthorized memory access without compromising latency or task performance
relevance: The most explicit mapping of memory-stack design onto named regulatory instruments, including retention and least-privilege as first-class memory properties.

title: AI Agents Under EU Law
summary: First systematic regulatory mapping for AI agent providers, integrating draft harmonised standards under Standardisation Request M/613 to CEN/CENELEC JTC 21 as of January 2026, the GPAI Code of Practice of July 2025, the CRA harmonised standards programme under Mandate M/606, and the November 2025 Digital Omnibus proposals. Presents a taxonomy of nine agent deployment categories mapping concrete actions to regulatory triggers, identifies agent-specific compliance challenges in cybersecurity, human oversight, transparency across multi-party action chains and runtime behavioural drift, and proposes a twelve-step compliance architecture.
key_claims: Taxonomy of nine agent deployment categories mapping actions to regulatory triggers
Agent-specific compliance challenges include human oversight, transparency across multi-party action chains and runtime behavioural drift
Concludes high-risk agentic systems with untraceable behavioural drift cannot currently satisfy the AI Act's essential requirements
The provider's foundational compliance task is an exhaustive inventory of the agent's external actions, data flows, connected systems and affected persons
Providers face simultaneous obligations under the AI Act, GDPR, CRA, DSA, Data Act, DGA, NIS2 and the revised Product Liability Directive
relevance: The 'untraceable behavioural drift' conclusion makes memory provenance a compliance requirement rather than a nice-to-have for high-risk agentic deployments.

verification.notes: Nannini et al., 6 Apr 2026. Abstract confirms the conclusion that high-risk agentic systems with untraceable behavioural drift cannot currently satisfy the AI Act.

title: AgentRiskBOM: A Risk-Scoping Security Bill of Materials for Agentic AI Systems
summary: Security bill of materials for tool-using AI agents, layered additively over SBOM, AIBOM and MLBOM and adding fields for runtime authority: autonomy, tool permissions, memory, credential scope, approval gates, audit signals, inter-agent communication and external action capability. Implemented as a JSON-schema artifact with corpus, scenarios, scorer, diff detector, control mapper and reports; validated on 13 open-source agents and 52 risk scenarios across 14 categories, giving 100% risk-category visibility versus 10.5% for SBOM-like and 20.9% for AIBOM-like views, with a diff detector correctly identifying all 33 injected deployment mutations.
key_claims: Names 'capability opacity': the absence of a structured account of what an agent can access, remember, change, delegate and prove afterward
Memory and approval gates are first-class declared fields alongside tool permissions and credential scope
Native-equivalent coverage score 14 of 16 capability dimensions vs 1 for SBOM, 1.5 AIBOM, 2 MLBOM
100% risk-category visibility vs 10.5% SBOM-like and 20.9% AIBOM-like across 52 scenarios
Diff detector identifies the correct change type for all 33 injected deployment mutations
