verification.notes: Paper confirmed (arXiv:2606.21877, Dutta & Moharil). Abstract confirms 13 open-source agents, 52 risk scenarios across 14 categories, and the native-equivalent coverage score of 14 across 16 dimensions vs 1.0 SBOM / 1.5 AI-BOM / 2.0 ML-BOM. NOT FOUND on the page: '100% risk-category visibility vs 10.5% SBOM-like and 20.9% AIBOM-like' and 'all 33 injected deployment mutations'. These are body-level claims I could not locate; treat as unverified.

title: Runtime Compliance Verification for AI Agents
summary: C-Trace expresses a subset of GDPR requirements — consent, purpose limitation, data minimization and the right to erasure — as formal policy predicates over agent execution traces, uses a runtime monitor intercepting every tool invocation and model output to reject non-compliant actions, and tests the agent with attack dialogues including DSPy-generated and red-teaming-corpus prompts. Under 10% per-category extractor noise the monitor holds attack success at or below 12% and false positives at or below 16%, reaching 0% attack success under perfect extraction.
key_claims: GDPR consent, purpose limitation, data minimization and right to erasure formalized as predicates over agent execution traces
Runtime monitor intercepts every tool invocation and model output and rejects non-compliant actions
Under 10% per-category extractor noise: attack success <=12%, false positives <=16%
0% attack success rate under perfect extraction
Evaluated on four case studies reframed to GDPR
relevance: Shows the right to erasure can be enforced over agent traces mechanically — the technical shape a revocation mechanism for agent memory would take.

verification.notes: Kahani, Barati, Addae; 17 Jun 2026. Abstract confirms C-Trace, GDPR predicates over execution traces, runtime monitor, DSPy-generated attack dialogues.

title: MemAudit: Post-hoc Auditing of Poisoned Agent Memory via Causal Attribution and Structural Anomaly Detection
summary: Post-hoc causal memory auditing framework answering which stored memories are responsible after harmful behaviour has already occurred, combining a counterfactual memory influence score measuring each memory's causal contribution to harmful outputs with a memory consistency graph identifying structurally anomalous entries. Evaluated against MINJA, a query-only memory injection attack, it reduces QA attack success from 70% to 0% and RAP reasoning-agent attack success from 83.3% to 0% under realistic post-hoc auditing.
key_claims: Existing defenses focus on online intervention and do not answer which stored memories caused observed harm
Combines counterfactual memory influence scoring with a memory consistency graph
QA attack success reduced from 70% to 0%; RAP attack success from 83.3% to 0%
Evaluated against MINJA query-only memory injection
relevance: The auditability leg of the policy question: after an incident, attribution back to specific memory entries is technically feasible, which is what revocation requires.

verification.notes: Paper confirmed (arXiv:2605.23723v1, 22 May 2026, Tan et al.) with the correct title and the counterfactual-influence + structural-anomaly method. NOT FOUND: the record's 'QA attack success reduced from 70% to 0%; RAP attack success from 83.3% to 0%' and the MINJA evaluation do not appear in the retrievable abstract (the served abstract is truncated after the threat-model sentence). Treat these figures as unverified.

title: Don't Let AI Agents YOLO Your Files: Shifting Information and Control to Filesystems for Agent Safety and Autonomy
summary: First systematic study of agent filesystem misuse, analysing 290 public reports across 13 frameworks, finding agents have limited information about their filesystem effects and insufficient control over them. YoloFS is an agent-native filesystem with staging (all mutations isolated before commit, giving users corrective control), snapshots (extending that control to agents for self-correction) and progressive permission (preventive control gating access with minimal interaction). On 11 tasks with hidden side effects YoloFS enables agent self-correction in 8 while keeping all effects staged and reviewable; on 112 routine tasks it requires fewer user interactions while matching baseline success rate.
key_claims: 290 public reports of agent filesystem misuse across 13 frameworks analyzed
Current approaches force a tradeoff between unrestricted access and burdensome permission prompts
On 11 tasks with hidden side effects, agent self-correction enabled in 8 with all effects staged and reviewable
On 112 routine tasks, fewer user interactions than baseline while matching success rate
relevance: Demonstrates staged-then-committed writes as a review model that lowers rather than raises human burden — the rare counterexample to the review-capacity constraint, directly applicable to memory-file writes.

verification.notes: Zhong et al., 15 Apr 2026 (v3 13 Aug 2026). Abstract confirms 290 public reports, self-correction on 8 of 11 hidden-side-effect tasks, and reduced interactions on 112 routine tasks.

title: Human-AI Synergy in Agentic Code Review
summary: Large-scale empirical analysis of 278,790 code review conversations across 300 open-source GitHub projects comparing human reviewer and AI agent feedback and human-AI collaboration patterns. Human reviewers provide additional feedback categories including understanding, testing and knowledge transfer, and exchange 11.8% more rounds when reviewing AI-generated code than human-written code. AI agent code suggestions are adopted at a significantly lower rate than human ones, over half of unadopted AI suggestions are incorrect or superseded by alternative fixes, and adopted AI suggestions produce significantly larger increases in code complexity and size.
key_claims: 278,790 code review conversations across 300 open-source GitHub projects
Human reviewers exchange 11.8% more rounds when reviewing AI-generated code than human-written code
AI agent suggestions are adopted into the codebase at a significantly lower rate than human suggestions
Over half of unadopted AI suggestions are incorrect or addressed through alternative fixes
Adopted AI suggestions produce significantly larger increases in code complexity and code size
relevance: Quantifies the review-overhead multiplier for agent output, which is the cost side of routing agent-written memory through the same human review pipeline.

title: Ground Truth First: A Longitudinal Evaluation Instrument for Agent Memory, and the Tenure Crossover in Memory-Architecture Rankings
summary: Inverts the usual benchmark pipeline: a seeded life-script sampler emits facts with validity intervals, volatility classes and source channels before any text exists, an LLM renderer writes chat and email from per-event fact manifests, a fidelity verifier confirms every planted fact, and questions are instantiated mechanically so gold answers are script-valid by construction. Benchmarking five memory architectures against a no-memory control at two horizons finds backend rankings invert with history length — the budgeted curated-map memory leading at three weeks falls from 96% to 72% recall of evicted content by nine weeks while a provenance-typed graph rises to 90% (exact p=0.031) — and that write-stage quality strongly correlates with downstream quality (weakly-written facts fail 24% vs 2%).
key_claims: Corpus of ~380 questions across 15 types with per-fact validity intervals, sent/received trust distinctions and injection probes
Memory-architecture rankings invert with history length: curated-map memory falls 96% -> 72% recall by nine weeks while a provenance-typed graph rises to 90% (exact p=0.031)
Write-stage quality strongly correlates with downstream quality: weakly-written facts fail 24% vs 2%
Injection resistance tracks whether provenance boundaries survive the representation
A full-rendered-history baseline ties or exceeds the best memory system at short horizon but shows no judge-independent advantage at nine weeks, at about twice the read cost
relevance: The write-quality-predicts-downstream-quality result is the strongest general argument for investing in the write gate, and the tenure crossover warns that short-horizon evaluations mis-rank memory designs.

title: Memory Sandbox: Transparent and Interactive Memory Management for Conversational Agents
authors_or_org: Ziheng Huang, Sebastian Gutierrez, Hemanth Kamana, Stephen MacNeil
summary: Interactive system and design probe letting users manage the conversational memory of LLM-powered agents. Treats memories as data objects that can be viewed, manipulated, recorded, summarized and shared across conversations. Motivated by the observation that users lack affordances for seeing and controlling what the agent remembers, producing poor mental models and conversational breakdowns.
key_claims: Users currently lack affordances for viewing and controlling what an agent remembers, causing poor mental models and conversational breakdowns
Memories can be made first-class manipulable data objects: view, edit, record, summarize, share across conversations
Design probe rather than controlled evaluation
Users currently lack affordances for viewing and controlling what the agent remembers, producing poor mental models and breakdowns
Memories treated as manipulable data objects, shareable across conversations
relevance: The origin point of the memory-editing-UI line and the canonical statement that memory transparency is an interaction-design problem, not only a systems problem.

verification.notes: Huang, Gutierrez, Kamana, MacNeil; 3 Aug 2023. Abstract confirms memories as manipulable data objects and the design-probe framing.

title: RepoAgent: An LLM-Powered Open-Source Framework for Repository-level Code Documentation Generation
authors_or_org: Qinyu Luo, Yining Ye, Shihao Liang, Zhong Zhang, Yujia Qin, Yaxi Lu, Yesai Wu, Xin Cong, Yankai Lin, Yingli Zhang, Xiaoyin Che, Zhiyuan Liu, Maosong Sun
summary: RepoAgent is an open-source LLM-powered framework that proactively generates, maintains, and updates repository-level code documentation. The authors report qualitative and quantitative evaluations showing it produces high-quality repository-level documentation. Code and results are released at https://github.com/OpenBMB/RepoAgent.
key_claims: LLM use for code documentation generation remains underexplored relative to code generation and debugging
RepoAgent proactively generates, maintains, and updates documentation rather than producing it once
Qualitative and quantitative evaluation is claimed to validate high-quality repository-level documentation (no headline numbers stated on the abs page)
relevance: An early exemplar of the documentation-as-memory pattern: durable, agent-written, in-repo artifacts that persist project knowledge across sessions rather than living in a context window. Establishes the maintenance/update problem later benchmarked by SWD-Bench and RepoDoc.

title: ReadMe.LLM: A Framework to Help LLMs Understand Your Library
authors_or_org: Sandya Wijaya, Jacob Bolano, Alejandro Gomez Soteres, Shriyanshu Kode, Yue Huang, Anant Sahai
summary: ReadMe.LLM proposes LLM-oriented documentation maintained by library authors alongside traditional software updates, distinct from human-oriented docs. Attaching ReadMe.LLM content to a query raises code-generation accuracy on niche libraries, in one case study to 100% success across all tested models. The paper presents two practical applications across diverse libraries and argues the approach generalizes across programming domains.
key_claims: Existing human-oriented documentation can fail for niche libraries even when the LLM has web search and the library is documented online
Attaching ReadMe.LLM to a query improves performance to near-perfect accuracy; one case study reached up to 100% success across all tested models
Proposes a software development lifecycle where LLM-specific documentation is maintained alongside traditional software updates
relevance: A human-authored, in-repo context surface written specifically for machine readers — the library-side analogue of AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md. Evidence that who writes the memory (library maintainers, not the agent) can matter more than retrieval machinery.

title: CodeWiki: Evaluating AI's Ability to Generate Holistic Documentation for Large-Scale Codebases
authors_or_org: Anh Nguyen Hoang, Minh Le-Anh, Bach Le, Nghi D. Q. Bui
summary: CodeWiki is a framework for generating holistic, repository-level documentation across seven programming languages, combining hierarchical decomposition that preserves architectural context, recursive multi-agent processing with dynamic task delegation, and multi-modal synthesis with diagrams and data-flow representations. The authors also introduce CodeWikiBench, an evaluation harness with multi-dimensional rubrics and LLM-based assessment protocols. CodeWiki scores 68.79% quality versus the DeepWiki baseline's 64.06%.
key_claims: CodeWiki achieves 68.79% quality score vs DeepWiki baseline 64.06% (a 4.73% improvement)
Improvement is strongest on scripting languages (+10.47%)
Supports seven programming languages; introduces CodeWikiBench with multi-dimensional rubrics and LLM-as-judge protocols
Targets cross-file, cross-module and system-level interactions rather than local artifacts
relevance: Makes generated repository wikis a measurable artifact class, and directly benchmarks the industry incumbent (DeepWiki). Relevant to whether agent-written documentation is a viable durable memory substrate and how its quality is judged.

title: CodeMEM: AST-Guided Adaptive Memory for Repository-Level Iterative Code Generation
authors_or_org: Peiding Wang, Li Zhang, Fang Liu, Chongyang Tao, Yinghao Zhu
summary: CodeMEM manages memory for repository-level iterative code generation with two components: a Code Context Memory that dynamically maintains and updates repository context through AST-guided LLM operations, and a Code Session Memory that builds a code-centric representation of interaction history and explicitly detects and mitigates forgetting via AST-based analysis. The authors argue existing memory approaches are limited by natural-language-centric representations. Evaluation is on CodeIF-Bench and CoderEval.
key_claims: Improves instruction following by 12.2% for the current turn and 11.5% at session level
Reduces interaction rounds by 2-3 while keeping competitive inference latency
Outperforms baselines on CodeIF-Bench and CoderEval
Expanding session history leads to forgetting of previously resolved errors; AST-based analysis is used to detect and mitigate it
relevance: A code-structured (rather than prose) memory representation for the within-session horizon, with an explicit forgetting-detection mechanism. Evidence for the claim that SE-specific memory should be typed to code artifacts, not free text.

title: Contextual Memory Virtualisation: DAG-Based State Management and Structurally Lossless Trimming for LLM Agents
summary: Contextual Memory Virtualisation (CMV) treats accumulated LLM understanding as version-controlled state, borrowing from OS virtual memory: session history is modelled as a Directed Acyclic Graph with formally defined snapshot, branch and trim primitives that enable context reuse across independent parallel sessions. A three-pass structurally lossless trimming algorithm preserves every user message and assistant response verbatim while stripping mechanical bloat (raw tool outputs, base64 images, metadata). Evaluation is a single-user case study over 76 real-world coding sessions.
key_claims: Trimming reduces token counts by a mean of 20% and up to 86% for sessions with significant overhead, while preserving user and assistant messages verbatim
Mixed tool-use sessions average 39% reduction and reach break-even within 10 turns under prompt caching
Evaluated on 76 real-world coding sessions (single-user case study)
Frames lossy compaction at context limits as the mechanism by which architectural mappings, trade-off decisions and codebase conventions are lost
relevance: Positions compaction loss as a systems problem with a lossless alternative, and gives field measurements from real coding sessions. Directly bears on the memory-track question of what is destroyed at compaction and who decides.

title: Building Effective AI Coding Agents for the Terminal: Scaffolding, Harness, Context Engineering, and Lessons Learned
summary: OPENDEV is an open-source, Rust-based command-line coding agent presented as a blueprint for terminal-native autonomous software engineering. Its architecture combines workload-specialized model routing, a dual-agent split of planning from execution, lazy tool discovery, and adaptive context compaction that progressively reduces older observations. It adds an automated memory system that accumulates project-specific knowledge across sessions and counters instruction fade-out through event-driven system reminders.
key_claims: Employs an automated memory system to accumulate project-specific knowledge across sessions
Counteracts instruction fade-out through event-driven system reminders
Uses adaptive context compaction that progressively reduces older observations to prevent context bloat and reasoning degradation
Described as work in progress with continuous updates; no headline benchmark numbers reported on the abs page
relevance: A harness-side account of cross-session memory written by the agent itself, plus the 'instruction fade-out' framing that motivates event-driven reminders. Useful primary evidence for how memory and reminder machinery are actually wired in a CLI agent.

title: Evaluating Repository-level Software Documentation via Question Answering and Feature-Driven Development
authors_or_org: Xinchen Wang, Ruida Hu, Cuiyun Gao, Pengfei Gao, Chao Peng
summary: SWD-Bench evaluates repository-level software documentation not by scoring text directly but by measuring whether an LLM can understand and implement functionality using it, via three function-driven QA tasks: Functionality Detection, Functionality Localization, and Functionality Completion. The benchmark contains 4,170 entries mined from high-quality pull requests and enriched with repository-level context. Experiments expose limitations of current documentation generation methods and show source code provides complementary value.
key_claims: SWD-Bench contains 4,170 entries mined from high-quality Pull Requests with repository-level context
Documentation from the best-performing generation method improves SWE-Agent's issue-solving rate by 20.00%
Argues LLM-as-a-judge evaluation of documentation suffers from vague criteria and limited repository-level knowledge
Three interconnected QA tasks: Functionality Detection, Localization, and Completion
relevance: The strongest downstream-utility measurement of documentation-as-memory: it evaluates written project knowledge by whether it makes an agent solve issues better (+20.00%), rather than by judged prose quality. A template for measuring memory by task effect.

title: RepoDoc: A Knowledge Graph-Based Framework to Automatic Documentation Generation and Incremental Updates
authors_or_org: Dong Xu, Mingwei Liu, Xiwen Wang, Jianfeng Zhong, Zibin Zheng
summary: RepoDoc uses a repository knowledge graph (RepoKG) as the semantic foundation for the whole documentation lifecycle, in three stages: RepoKG construction, module clustering into functionally cohesive hierarchical units, and agent-based generation that queries the graph to produce modular, cross-referenced documentation with auto-generated Mermaid diagrams. For maintenance, a semantic impact propagation mechanism navigates the RepoKG bidirectionally to pinpoint affected parts and regenerate selectively. Evaluated on 24 repositories across 8 programming languages.
key_claims: Improves API coverage by 32.5% and completeness by 10.4% over state-of-the-art alternatives
Generates documentation 3x faster with 85% fewer tokens
For incremental updates: 73% less update time, 77% less token usage, and 10.2% higher update recall
Evaluated on 24 repositories across 8 programming languages
relevance: Tackles the staleness problem that makes documentation-as-memory fail: selective, impact-propagated regeneration rather than wholesale rewrite. The incremental-update metrics are the memory-maintenance cost numbers the track needs.

title: From Unstructured Recall to Schema-Grounded Memory: Reliable AI Memory via Iterative, Schema-Aware Extraction
authors_or_org: Alex Petrov, Alexander Gusak, Denis Mukha, Dima Korolev
summary: xmemory argues that embedding text and searching semantically fails for precise facts, state tracking and logical operations, and proposes schema-grounded memory in which information is structured at ingestion rather than at retrieval. The write path is decomposed into three stages — detecting relevant entities, identifying present fields, and extracting validated values — with validation checkpoints and targeted retries to stop cascading errors. The authors report that architecting the write operation yields more reliability than larger models or bigger retrieval.
key_claims: 97.10% F1 on end-to-end memory operations, versus Mem0 at 87.24% F1
90.42% object-level extraction accuracy under human-judge oversight
95.2% accuracy on a real-world financial transaction task
Careful architecture of the memory write path beats simply using more powerful models or larger retrieval
relevance: Puts validation on the write path rather than the read path — the central design question of who checks memory before it is stored. Its schema-plus-retry gating is the machine-side counterpart to human pre-write approval.

title: Context-as-AI-Service: Surfacing Cross-File Dependency Chains for LLM-Generated Developer Documentation
authors_or_org: Ameya Gawde, Vyzantinos Repantis, Harshvardhan Singh, Lucy Moys
summary: CAIS is a retrieval layer that lets LLM agents find and fix cross-file dependency problems in developer documentation. It indexes source code, API references and upstream documentation, and agents query it through tool calls combining keyword and semantic search. Evaluated on a production SDK with Claude Sonnet 4.6, CAIS-augmented agents caught documentation errors the baseline missed.
key_claims: CAIS-augmented agents detected 2 factual inaccuracies and 2 underspecified comments in API reviews, plus 1 executable bug and 2 missing prerequisites in tutorial validation, that the baseline missed
22-34% reductions in wall-clock time and lower token usage
Addresses the 'cross-file documentation problem' where claims look correct in isolation but conflict with distributed codebase logic
Evaluated on a production SDK using Claude Sonnet 4.6
relevance: Treats project context as a queried service rather than a file the agent reads — an architectural alternative to in-repo context files, with measured effects on documentation accuracy and cost.

title: User as Code: Executable Memory for Personalized Agents
summary: User as Code (UaC) represents persistent user memory as executable Python: typed objects hold state and functions encode behavioural rules, replacing unstructured text, knowledge graphs or flat fact stores consulted by retrieval. Memory is an append-only log that never discards a fact, periodically checkpointed into typed code. The advantage shows most on aggregate queries, where computation over typed state beats retrieval, and deterministic rule execution supports proactive safety alerts such as flagging drug-allergy interactions discovered months apart.
key_claims: 78.8% recall on the LOCOMO benchmark, matching prior systems
On aggregate queries (e.g. 'how many international trips last year?') retrieval-based memory scores 6-43% while UaC reaches 99% accuracy
Uses an append-only log that never discards a fact, periodically checkpointed into typed code
Deterministic rule execution enables proactive alerts across facts learned months apart
relevance: The strongest statement of code-as-memory-representation: memory that is executed rather than retrieved, with append-only write semantics. Relevant to whether SE agent memory should be typed and checkpointed instead of summarised prose.

title: Shared Selective Persistent Memory for Agentic LLM Systems
authors_or_org: Sanjana Pedada, Aditya Dhavala, Neelraj Patil
summary: This work addresses the fact that agentic LLM systems generating code via multi-turn tool use discard configuration choices, domain constraints, data schemas and tool-use patterns at every new session. The proposed architecture selectively retains four categories of reusable context — task specifications, data schemas, tool configurations and output constraints — while discarding session-specific reasoning, and shares that memory across users under role-based access controls. It was deployed on a collaborative platform where agents produce git-versioned artifacts from heterogeneous data sources.
key_claims: 96% task completion with selective persistent memory, versus 79% with no memory and 71% with full history — full-history persistence degrades performance
14x reduction in task time through a zero-token refresh mechanism
97x reduction in per-invocation token cost via summary-driven generation versus raw data injection
Zero-token refresh succeeded in 12/12 trials across public datasets
Memory is shareable across users with role-based access controls
relevance: Rare quantitative evidence that keeping everything is worse than keeping the right four categories (71% full history vs 96% selective), plus an access-control model for memory shared between developers. Central to the 'what should be written' half of the memory thesis.

title: Designing meaningful human oversight in AI
summary: This paper proposes a layered-agency design framework distinguishing AI operative agency in task execution from human evaluative agency in verification, steering and substitution, arguing current oversight either strips AI of its agentic character or reduces humans to a rubber stamp. It reframes explainability around external reasoning faithfulness — alignment with externally articulated criteria and human expertise — rather than internal mechanistic transparency. It exploits the solve-verify asymmetry so humans can check and contest outputs without resolving the task themselves.
key_claims: Three contributions: a layered agency framework separating operative from evaluative agency; external rather than internal reasoning faithfulness as sufficient for oversight; a structured catalogue of oversight mechanisms
Oversight mechanisms catalogued include structured rationales, reasoning traces, confidence signals, policy attribution, circuit breakers and appeal bundles
Presents four end-to-end design patterns translating the principles into implementable system architectures
Outlines evaluation criteria for AI agency, human agency and joint system agency
relevance: Supplies the conceptual vocabulary for why memory approval must be cheap to verify: the solve-verify asymmetry is exactly the condition that makes pre-write approval of agent-written memory tractable or not.

title: On the Need to Rethink Trust in AI Assistants for Software Development: A Critical Review
summary: A cross-disciplinary literature review plus a critical review of recent SE articles on how trust is conceptualized in software engineering, HCI and information systems. The authors find that SE articles rarely define or conceptualize trust, and that SE research on AI assistants often equates trust with the likelihood of accepting generated content — which does not capture trust's conceptual complexity and makes true secondary research impossible. They report a significant maturity gap versus related disciplines, which distinguish initial trust from trust formation and appropriate from inappropriate trust.
key_claims: SE research frequently equates trust with acceptance of generated content; trust is rarely explicitly defined in SE articles
Related disciplines embed methodology in established trust models, distinguishing initial trust from trust formation and appropriate from inappropriate trust
Reveals a significant maturity gap in SE trust research compared with HCI, information systems, psychology and philosophy
Provides concrete recommendations for adopting established trust models and instruments beyond artifact acceptance
relevance: A methodological warning for the memory track: studies that measure whether developers accept agent-written memory are measuring acceptance, not trust. Constrains how HITL/approval findings in this corpus can be interpreted.

title: Improving LLM-assisted code generation through the use of architectural documents and implementation plans
venue: Proceedings of the 3rd International Workshop on Designing Software
summary: Building on prior work that guides LLMs through Attribute-Driven Design (ADD), this paper treats architectural documentation as a first-class input to LLM-assisted code generation. The proposed workflow has the LLM synthesize an implementation plan from requirements and an architecture document, then generate code with human oversight. Using a ReAct-style agent as a case study, the authors run three experiments evaluating architectural conformance and functional correctness of a primary use case, plus size and modularity metrics via the DV8 tool.
key_claims: Incorporating architectural documentation substantially improves architectural conformance
Adding an explicit implementation plan further enhances functional correctness and modularity
Three experiments with a ReAct-style agent; size and modularity measured with the DV8 tool
Code generation happens with human oversight in the proposed workflow
relevance: Evidence that human-authored architecture documents plus a derived plan function as durable design memory that measurably constrains agent output — the human-authored end of the write-policy spectrum.

title: CIAO - Code In Architecture Out - Automated Software Architecture Documentation with Large Language Models
venue: 2026 IEEE 23rd International Conference on Software Architecture (ICSA)
summary: CIAO defines an LLM-based workflow that takes a GitHub repository as input and produces system-level architectural documentation following a template derived from ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010, SEI Views & Beyond and the C4 model, and the result can be added directly to the target repository. The authors evaluate it with 22 developers, each reviewing documentation generated for a repository they had contributed to. Developers generally found the documentation valuable, comprehensible and broadly accurate, while flagging limits in diagram quality, high-level context modeling and deployment views.
key_claims: Evaluated with 22 developers reviewing documentation for repositories they had contributed to
Developers perceive generated documentation as valuable, comprehensible and broadly accurate with respect to source code
Limitations identified in diagram quality, high-level context modeling, and deployment views
Generating a complete architectural document takes only a few minutes and is inexpensive to run
Template derived from ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010, SEI Views & Beyond, and the C4 model
relevance: One of the few documentation-generation studies with real contributor review of their own repositories, giving human-judged accuracy for agent-written architecture memory and naming where it systematically fails.
